lessons.title: Waves and Types of Waves
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Wave?

When a disturbance is produced in a medium and energy travels from one place to another without the transfer of matter, it is called a wave. For example: when a stone is thrown into a pond, water waves reach the shore, but the water particles do not move forward — only energy travels forward.

Mechanical Waves

Waves that need a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel are mechanical waves. Examples: water waves, sound waves, waves on a rope and on a spring. They cannot travel in a vacuum.

Transverse Wave

A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel of the wave. It is made up of crests and troughs.

  • Crest — the highest point of the wave
  • Trough — the lowest point of the wave
  • Examples: water waves, light waves

Longitudinal Wave

A wave in which the particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction of travel of the wave. It is made up of compressions and rarefactions.

  • Compression — the part where the particles are close together and the pressure is high
  • Rarefaction — the part where the particles are far apart and the pressure is low
  • Examples: sound waves, waves on a spring (Slinky)

Electromagnetic Waves

Light, radio waves and microwaves are electromagnetic waves. They need no medium; they travel even in a vacuum at a speed of 3 × 10^8 m/s.

mcqs.q: When a disturbance is produced in a medium and energy travels from one place to another without transfer of matter, it is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a wave. In a wave, energy travels forward through the medium, but the particles of the medium do not move forward with it. For example, when a stone is thrown into a pond, the water waves reach the shore while the water particles stay in place.

mcqs.q: Which of the following waves needs a material medium to travel?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is sound waves. Sound is a mechanical wave, and mechanical waves need a material medium such as a solid, liquid or gas to travel. They cannot travel in a vacuum, unlike light and radio waves which are electromagnetic.

mcqs.q: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium vibrate:
options: They do not vibrate at all
Perpendicular to the direction of the wave
Parallel to the direction of the wave
mcqs.why: The correct answer is perpendicular to the direction of travel of the wave. A transverse wave is made up of crests and troughs because its particles move up and down at right angles to the wave's direction. Water waves and light waves are examples of transverse waves.

mcqs.q: The highest point of a transverse wave is called the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the crest. The crest is the highest point of a transverse wave, while the trough is its lowest point. Compressions and rarefactions belong to longitudinal waves, not to transverse waves.

mcqs.q: A longitudinal wave is made up of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is compressions and rarefactions. In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction of the wave, so regions where particles are close together (compressions) and far apart (rarefactions) are formed. Sound waves and waves on a spring are examples.

mcqs.q: In a compression of a longitudinal wave:
options: Particles are far apart and pressure is low
Particles are close together and pressure is high
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the particles are close together and the pressure is high. A compression is the crowded part of a longitudinal wave. The opposite region, where particles are far apart and pressure is low, is called a rarefaction.

mcqs.q: Which pair contains only longitudinal waves?
options: Sound waves and waves on a spring
mcqs.why: The correct answer is sound waves and waves on a spring (a Slinky). In both of these, the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions. Water waves and light waves are transverse waves, so the other options are wrong.

mcqs.q: Electromagnetic waves travel in a vacuum at a speed of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 3 x 10^8 m/s. Light, radio waves and microwaves are electromagnetic waves; they need no medium and travel even in a vacuum at this speed. The value 340 m/s is roughly the speed of sound in air, not of electromagnetic waves.

mcqs.q: When a stone is thrown into a pond, the water particles:
options: Sink to the bottom of the pond
Move forward to the shore with the wave
Do not move forward; only energy travels
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the water particles do not move forward; only energy travels forward. This is the basic property of a wave: it transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter. The ripples reach the shore, but the water itself stays where it is.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a mechanical wave?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the light wave. Light is an electromagnetic wave, which needs no material medium and can travel in a vacuum. Water waves, waves on a rope and sound waves are mechanical waves because they all need a medium.

lessons.title: Wave Properties and the Wave Equation
lessons.notes_html:
Basic Properties of a Wave

  • Amplitude — maximum displacement from the equilibrium position; unit metre (m)
  • Period (T) — time for one complete vibration; unit second (s)
  • Frequency (f) — number of complete vibrations in one second; unit hertz (Hz)
  • Wavelength (λ) — length of one complete wave; unit metre (m)

Relation between period and frequency:

f = 1 / T

The Wave Equation

Speed of wave = frequency × wavelength:

v = f λ

Worked Example 1

A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 1300 kHz. The speed of radio waves is 3 × 10^8 m/s. Find the wavelength.

Given: f = 1300 kHz = 1.3 × 10^6 Hz, v = 3 × 10^8 m/s

λ = v / f = (3 × 10^8) / (1.3 × 10^6) = 230.77 m

Worked Example 2

Water waves have a wavelength of 1.6 m and a frequency of 0.80 Hz. Find their speed.

v = f λ = 0.80 × 1.6 = 1.28 m/s

Ripple Tank and Wave Front

A ripple tank is a shallow glass tray of water in which water waves are produced by a vibrating motor so that their properties can be observed. A wave front is the line joining all the points that are vibrating in the same phase.

Three Main Properties of Waves

PropertyMeaning
ReflectionThe wave strikes a barrier and returns back
RefractionThe wave bends as it passes from one medium to another; the speed and wavelength change but the frequency stays the same
DiffractionThe wave spreads out as it passes through a gap or opening

Water waves show all three properties. Going from deep water to shallow water, waves bend towards the normal and their wavelength decreases.

mcqs.q: The maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium position is called its:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is amplitude, and its unit is the metre (m). Amplitude measures how far the vibrating particles move from their rest position. Wavelength is the length of one complete wave, and period is the time for one complete vibration.

mcqs.q: Frequency is the number of complete vibrations in:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is one second, and the unit of frequency is the hertz (Hz). Frequency tells how many complete vibrations take place every second. It is related to the period by the equation f = 1 / T.

mcqs.q: If the period of a wave is 0.5 s, its frequency is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2 Hz. Frequency and period are related by f = 1 / T, so f = 1 / 0.5 = 2 Hz. A shorter period always means a higher frequency, because more vibrations fit into one second.

mcqs.q: The wave equation relating speed, frequency and wavelength is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is v = f lambda: the speed of a wave equals its frequency multiplied by its wavelength. This single equation can be rearranged to find any one of the three quantities when the other two are known. It applies to all kinds of waves.

mcqs.q: A radio station broadcasts at 1300 kHz. With wave speed 3 x 10^8 m/s, the wavelength is about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 230.77 m. Using lambda = v / f with f = 1300 kHz = 1.3 x 10^6 Hz gives lambda = (3 x 10^8) / (1.3 x 10^6) = 230.77 m. This is the worked example given in the notes for the wave equation.

mcqs.q: Water waves of wavelength 1.6 m and frequency 0.80 Hz have a speed of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 1.28 m/s. From the wave equation, v = f lambda = 0.80 x 1.6 = 1.28 m/s. Multiplying frequency by wavelength always gives the speed at which the wave pattern travels through the medium.

mcqs.q: A ripple tank is used to:
options: Produce water waves and observe their properties
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to produce water waves and observe their properties. A ripple tank is a shallow glass tray of water in which a vibrating motor produces waves. Water waves studied this way show reflection, refraction and diffraction clearly.

mcqs.q: A wave front is the line joining all points that are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is vibrating in the same phase. A wave front connects all the points of a wave that are moving together in the same state of vibration at the same time. It is a useful way of picturing how waves travel in a ripple tank.

mcqs.q: When waves pass from deep water to shallow water, they:
options: Speed up and bend away from the normal
Bend towards the normal and their wavelength decreases
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they bend towards the normal and their wavelength decreases. This bending is refraction: as the wave enters shallow water its speed and wavelength change, but its frequency stays the same. The change of direction is towards the normal line.

mcqs.q: During refraction of a wave, the quantity that stays the same is the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is frequency. In refraction the wave bends as it passes from one medium to another; its speed and wavelength change, but the frequency remains unchanged. The frequency is fixed by the source that produces the wave.

lessons.title: Simple Harmonic Motion, Simple Pendulum and Damped Oscillations
lessons.notes_html:
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)

Vibratory motion in which the acceleration of the body is always directed towards the mean (equilibrium) position and is directly proportional to the displacement from that position is called simple harmonic motion.

Conditions for SHM

  • The restoring force always pushes the body towards the mean position
  • The acceleration is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position

Simple Pendulum

A simple pendulum is made by hanging a small heavy bob from a light string. The component of the bob's weight acting along the arc acts as the restoring force, so the pendulum performs SHM.

Period of the pendulum:

T = 2π √(L / g)

  • The period depends only on the length L of the string and on g, not on the mass of the bob
  • At the mean position the speed is greatest and the acceleration is zero
  • At the extreme points the speed is zero and the acceleration is greatest
  • A second's pendulum has a period of 2 s and a frequency of 0.5 Hz

Worked Example

The string of a simple pendulum is 80.0 cm long. g = 9.8 m/s². Find its period and frequency.

L = 80.0 cm = 0.80 m

T = 2π √(0.80 / 9.8) = 2 × 3.14 × 0.286 = 1.79 s

f = 1 / T = 1 / 1.79 = 0.56 Hz

Ball and Bowl System

When a ball placed in a bowl is displaced to one side, it performs SHM about the bottom (mean position). The ball is fastest at the bottom and comes to rest for an instant at the two extreme points. The component of its weight along the slope pulls it back; the normal force only balances the perpendicular component of the weight.

Damped Oscillations

Oscillations whose amplitude gradually decreases because of friction and air resistance are called damped oscillations. Example: the sound of a drum skin gradually fading away. If the vibration were not damped, the sound would continue at the same loudness.

mcqs.q: In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration of the body is always directed towards:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the mean (equilibrium) position. In SHM the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position and is always directed towards it. This happens because the restoring force always pushes the body back towards the mean position.

mcqs.q: The period of a simple pendulum depends on:
options: The size of the bob only
The mass of the bob only
The length of the string and g only
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the length L of the string and g only, as shown by T = 2pi sqrt(L / g). The period does not depend on the mass of the bob. A longer string gives a longer period, while the mass can be changed without affecting T.

mcqs.q: A second's pendulum has a period of 2 s. Its frequency is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 0.5 Hz. Frequency is the reciprocal of the period, f = 1 / T = 1 / 2 = 0.5 Hz. A second's pendulum completes half a vibration in each second, swinging from one side to the other in one second.

mcqs.q: For a pendulum with string length 0.80 m and g = 9.8 m/s^2, the period is about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 1.79 s. Using T = 2pi sqrt(L / g) = 2 x 3.14 x sqrt(0.80 / 9.8) = 2 x 3.14 x 0.286 = 1.79 s. Its frequency is then f = 1 / 1.79 = 0.56 Hz, as worked out in the notes.

mcqs.q: At the mean position of a pendulum, the speed is ______ and the acceleration is ______.
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: speed is greatest and acceleration is zero at the mean position. As the bob passes through the bottom of its swing it moves fastest, and because displacement is zero there, the acceleration is also zero. At the extreme points the reverse is true.

mcqs.q: At the extreme points of a pendulum's swing:
options: Speed is greatest and acceleration is zero
Both speed and acceleration are zero
Speed is zero and acceleration is greatest
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the speed is zero and the acceleration is greatest at the extreme points. The bob stops for an instant at each end of the swing, and the displacement is largest there, so the restoring acceleration is also largest. It then accelerates back towards the mean position.

mcqs.q: In a simple pendulum, the restoring force is provided by:
options: The tension of the string alone
The component of the bob's weight acting along the arc
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the component of the bob's weight acting along the arc. A simple pendulum is a small heavy bob hung from a light string, and this component of weight pulls the bob back towards the mean position. That is why the pendulum performs simple harmonic motion.

mcqs.q: When a ball placed in a bowl is displaced to one side, it:
options: Performs SHM about the bottom (mean position)
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it performs SHM about the bottom of the bowl, which is its mean position. The ball is fastest at the bottom and comes to rest for an instant at the two extreme points. The component of its weight along the slope pulls it back each time.

mcqs.q: Damped oscillations are oscillations in which:
options: The amplitude gradually decreases due to friction and air resistance
The frequency becomes zero at once
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the amplitude gradually decreases because of friction and air resistance. An example is the sound of a drum skin gradually fading away. If the vibration were not damped, the sound would continue at the same loudness.

mcqs.q: One condition for simple harmonic motion is that:
options: There is no force on the body
The restoring force always pushes the body towards the mean position
The acceleration is constant in direction and size
The restoring force pushes the body away from the mean position
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the restoring force always pushes the body towards the mean position. Together with acceleration being proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position, this defines SHM. Without such a restoring force, the motion would not be simple harmonic.

lessons.title: Production and Nature of Sound
lessons.notes_html:
How is Sound Produced?

Sound is a form of energy produced by a vibrating body. When a body vibrates, it produces compressions and rarefactions in the air around it, and sound travels forward as a longitudinal wave.

Sound is a Mechanical Wave

Sound needs a material medium to travel, so it is a mechanical wave. The bell-jar experiment proves that sound does not travel in a vacuum: as the air is pumped out of the jar, the sound of the bell fades away and disappears.

Musical Sound and Noise

Musical SoundNoise
Produced by regular, periodic vibrationProduced by irregular vibration
Pleasant to hearUnpleasant to hear and harmful to health

Characteristics of Sound

  • Pitch — whether a sound is high or low; it depends on frequency. Higher frequency means higher pitch
  • Loudness — depends on amplitude
  • Quality — two instruments can be told apart because the shapes of their waves are different

Frequency Ranges

  • Audible sound — 20 Hz to 20 kHz, the range of the normal human ear
  • Infrasound — below 20 Hz
  • Ultrasound — above 20 kHz

mcqs.q: Sound is produced by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a vibrating body. Sound is a form of energy produced when a body vibrates; the vibrations produce compressions and rarefactions in the surrounding air. Without vibration, no sound is produced.

mcqs.q: Sound travels through air as:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a longitudinal wave. When a body vibrates, it produces compressions and rarefactions in the air, and sound travels forward in this form. In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel.

mcqs.q: The bell-jar experiment proves that:
options: Sound travels fastest in a vacuum
A bell cannot ring in air
Sound does not travel in a vacuum
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that sound does not travel in a vacuum. As air is pumped out of the bell jar, the sound of the bell inside fades away and disappears, because sound is a mechanical wave that needs a material medium. This confirms that a medium is essential for sound.

mcqs.q: Pitch of a sound depends on its:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is frequency: pitch tells whether a sound is high or low, and a higher frequency means a higher pitch. Loudness depends on amplitude instead, and quality depends on the shape of the wave. These are the three characteristics of sound given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Loudness of a sound depends on its:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is amplitude. A sound with a larger amplitude is louder, while a sound with a smaller amplitude is softer. Pitch, by contrast, depends on frequency, and quality depends on the shape of the wave produced.

mcqs.q: Two instruments playing the same note can be told apart because of the difference in:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the quality of the sound. Quality depends on the shape of the sound wave, which is different for each instrument. That is why a note sounds different on different instruments even when pitch and loudness are the same.

mcqs.q: Musical sound differs from noise because musical sound is produced by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is regular, periodic vibration, which makes musical sound pleasant to hear. Noise is produced by irregular vibration and is unpleasant to hear; it can even be harmful to health. This is the main difference between the two given in the notes.

mcqs.q: The range of audible sound for the normal human ear is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Sounds within this frequency range can be heard by a normal human ear. Sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound, and sounds above 20 kHz are called ultrasound, and neither can be heard.

mcqs.q: Sound with frequency below 20 Hz is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is infrasound. Infrasound lies below the audible range of 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so the human ear cannot detect it. Sound above 20 kHz is called ultrasound instead.

mcqs.q: Sound with frequency above 20 kHz is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is ultrasound. Ultrasound has a frequency higher than 20 kHz, above the upper limit of human hearing. It is used in sonar, medical scanning and cleaning delicate objects, as described later in this chapter.

lessons.title: Speed of Sound
lessons.notes_html:
Speed of Sound in Different Media

MediumSpeed (approx.)
Air (at 0°C)331 m/s
Water1480 m/s
Iron / SteelMore than about 5000 m/s

Sound travels fastest in solids, at a medium speed in liquids and slowest in gases, because the molecules of a solid are very close together and pass the vibration on quickly. Light is far faster than sound, so the flash of lightning is seen first and the thunder is heard afterwards.

Factors Affecting the Speed in Air

  • Temperature — the speed increases as the temperature rises; about 0.6 m/s for every 1°C rise
  • Humidity — sound travels faster in moist air than in dry air

Speed at any temperature:

v = 331 + 0.6 × T  (T = temperature in °C)

Worked Example 1

Find the speed of sound in air at 50°C, when the speed at 0°C is 331 m/s.

v = 331 + 0.6 × 50 = 331 + 30 = 361 m/s

Worked Example 2

The human hearing range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, find the difference between the wavelengths of these two frequencies.

λ1 = v / f1 = 340 / 20 = 17 m

λ2 = v / f2 = 340 / 20000 = 0.017 m

Difference = 17 − 0.017 = 16.98 m

mcqs.q: The speed of sound in air at 0 degrees C is about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 331 m/s. This is the standard value of the speed of sound in air at 0 degrees C used in the formula v = 331 + 0.6T. In water the speed is much higher, about 1480 m/s.

mcqs.q: Sound travels fastest in:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is solids, where the speed is more than about 5000 m/s in iron or steel. Sound travels at a medium speed in liquids and slowest in gases. This is because the molecules of a solid are very close together and pass the vibration on quickly.

mcqs.q: The flash of lightning is seen before the thunder is heard because:
options: Light is far faster than sound
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that light is far faster than sound. Both the flash and the thunder are produced at the same moment, but light reaches our eyes almost instantly while sound takes much longer. That is why there is a gap between seeing the flash and hearing the thunder.

mcqs.q: For every 1 degree C rise in temperature, the speed of sound in air increases by about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is about 0.6 m/s for every 1 degree C rise. This is built into the formula v = 331 + 0.6 x T, where T is the temperature in degrees C. At higher temperatures, therefore, sound travels faster in air.

mcqs.q: The speed of sound in air at 50 degrees C is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 361 m/s. Using v = 331 + 0.6 x T with T = 50 gives v = 331 + 30 = 361 m/s. This is the first worked example in the notes on the speed of sound.

mcqs.q: Sound travels faster in:
options: Dry air than in moist air
Cold air than in warm air
Moist air than in dry air
mcqs.why: The correct answer is moist air rather than dry air, because humidity increases the speed of sound. Temperature also increases the speed as it rises. Sound cannot travel in a vacuum at all, so the last option is impossible.

mcqs.q: If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, the wavelength of a 20 Hz sound is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 17 m. Using lambda = v / f = 340 / 20 = 17 m. This is the wavelength at the lowest audible frequency; at 20 kHz the wavelength is only 0.017 m, as shown in the notes.

mcqs.q: The wavelength of a 20 kHz sound at speed 340 m/s is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 0.017 m. From lambda = v / f = 340 / 20000 = 0.017 m. Comparing with the 17 m wavelength at 20 Hz, the difference between the two wavelengths is 16.98 m, as worked out in the notes.

mcqs.q: The speed of sound in water is about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is about 1480 m/s. Sound travels much faster in water than in air (331 m/s at 0 degrees C) because water is a liquid and its molecules are closer together. In iron or steel the speed is even higher, more than about 5000 m/s.

mcqs.q: The formula for the speed of sound in air at temperature T (in degrees C) is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is v = 331 + 0.6T. The value 331 m/s is the speed at 0 degrees C, and 0.6 m/s is added for each degree of temperature rise. For example, at 50 degrees C the speed becomes 361 m/s.

lessons.title: Echo, Sonar and Uses of Ultrasound
lessons.notes_html:
Echo

Sound returning after striking a barrier (a wall, a mountain, a building) is heard as an echo. An echo is a result of the reflection of sound.

  • For a clear echo the barrier must be at least about 17 m away
  • In a 10 m room no separate echo is heard, because the returning sound mixes with the original sound

Sonar

In sonar, ultrasound is sent out and the time of its echo is used to find the distance of objects under water or the depth of the sea.

Formula for depth:

d = (v × t) / 2

Worked Example

A ship measures the depth of the sea using ultrasound. The echo returns after 40 ms. The speed of sound in water is 1480 m/s. Find the depth.

t = 40 ms = 0.04 s

Total distance = v × t = 1480 × 0.04 = 59.2 m

Depth d = 59.2 / 2 = 29.6 m (halved because the sound goes down and comes back)

Uses of Ultrasound

  • Medical examination: forming images (scanning) of the internal parts of the body
  • Cleaning delicate objects and jewellery
  • Finding a crack or flaw in a metal block — the waves return early from the crack
  • In sonar, finding the depth of the sea and shoals of fish
  • A bat also finds the distance of its prey from the echo of its ultrasound

Worked Example 2

A bat emits sound of wavelength 0.0080 m. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. Find the frequency.

f = v / λ = 340 / 0.0080 = 42500 Hz = 42.5 kHz (ultrasound)

mcqs.q: An echo is produced by the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the reflection of sound. Sound returning after striking a barrier such as a wall, a mountain or a building is heard as an echo. It is the same reflection property that waves show in general, applied here to sound.

mcqs.q: For a clear echo, the barrier must be at least about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is about 17 m away. Only then does the returning sound reach the ear late enough to be heard separately from the original sound. In a 10 m room no separate echo is heard, because the returning sound mixes with the original sound.

mcqs.q: In sonar, the depth of the sea is found using:
options: Ultrasound and the time of its echo
mcqs.why: The correct answer is ultrasound and the time of its echo. Ultrasound is sent out from the ship, reflects from the sea bed or an object under water, and the measured echo time gives the distance. The formula used is d = (v x t) / 2.

mcqs.q: In the formula d = (v x t) / 2 for sonar depth, the division by 2 is because:
options: The sound goes down and comes back
The sound slows down in water
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the sound goes down and comes back, so the measured distance v x t is the total journey. Half of it is the actual depth. This halving step is essential in every echo-ranging calculation.

mcqs.q: A ship's ultrasound echo returns after 0.04 s. With sound speed 1480 m/s in water, the depth is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 29.6 m. The total distance is v x t = 1480 x 0.04 = 59.2 m, and the depth is half of this: 59.2 / 2 = 29.6 m. This is the worked sonar example given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT a use of ultrasound given in the notes?
options: Forming images of internal parts of the body
Finding a crack in a metal block
mcqs.why: The correct answer is heating food in an oven, which is done with microwaves, not ultrasound. Ultrasound is used for medical scanning, cleaning delicate objects and jewellery, finding flaws in metal blocks, and in sonar. Each of these uses depends on its echo or its fine vibrations.

mcqs.q: A bat finds the distance of its prey by using:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the echo of its ultrasound. A bat emits ultrasound and judges the distance of its prey from the returning echo, just like sonar. This works in complete darkness where eyesight is of little use.

mcqs.q: A bat emits sound of wavelength 0.0080 m. With sound speed 340 m/s, its frequency is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 42.5 kHz. Using f = v / lambda = 340 / 0.0080 = 42500 Hz = 42.5 kHz. Since this is above 20 kHz, the sound is ultrasound, which fits the way a bat locates its prey by echo.

mcqs.q: Ultrasound sent into a metal block returns early when it strikes:
options: A crack or flaw inside the block
The far end of the block
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a crack or flaw inside the block. The waves return early from the crack instead of travelling to the far end, which reveals the flaw without cutting the metal open. This is one of the important industrial uses of ultrasound.

mcqs.q: In a 10 m room, no separate echo is heard because:
options: The returning sound mixes with the original sound
The walls absorb all the sound
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the returning sound mixes with the original sound. A clear echo needs the barrier to be at least about 17 m away so that the reflected sound is delayed enough. In a small room the delay is too short for the ear to separate the two sounds.

lessons.title: Dispersion of Light and the Rainbow
lessons.notes_html:
What is Dispersion?

When white light passes through a glass prism, it splits into seven colours. This process is called the dispersion of light.

The Seven Colours

  • Violet — bends the most
  • Indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange
  • Red — bends the least

Each colour has a different wavelength and frequency, so in the prism each colour bends through a different angle. On entering the prism the speed and wavelength of the light change, but the frequency stays the same.

Luminous Body

A body that gives out its own light (the Sun, a bulb, a candle) is a luminous body. Light spreads from it in straight lines in all directions.

Rainbow

The rainbow seen in the sky after rain is a natural example of the dispersion of sunlight. The tiny water drops left in the air act as prisms: in each drop the light refracts, reflects inside and disperses, and is seen in seven colours. Each colour is linked to a particular frequency and wavelength.

mcqs.q: The splitting of white light into seven colours by a glass prism is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is dispersion. When white light passes through a glass prism, it splits into seven colours because each colour bends through a different angle. The rainbow is a natural example of this same effect.

mcqs.q: In the spectrum from a prism, the colour that bends the most is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is violet, which bends the most. Red bends the least, and the other colours (indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange) lie in between. Each colour has a different wavelength and frequency, so each bends by a different amount in the prism.

mcqs.q: The colour that bends the least in a prism is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is red. Red light is deviated through the smallest angle when white light is dispersed by a prism. Violet, at the other end of the spectrum, bends the most.

mcqs.q: When light enters a prism, which quantity stays the same?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is frequency. On entering the prism the speed and wavelength of the light change, but the frequency does not. Because the colours have different wavelengths, each one bends through a different angle and the spectrum is formed.

mcqs.q: A body that gives out its own light, such as the Sun or a candle, is called a:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a luminous body. The Sun, a bulb and a candle all give out their own light, and light spreads from such a body in straight lines in all directions. A body that does not give out its own light is non-luminous.

mcqs.q: A rainbow is formed because tiny water drops in the air act as:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is prisms. After rain, the tiny water drops left in the air refract the sunlight, reflect it inside and disperse it, so it is seen in seven colours. The rainbow is therefore a natural example of the dispersion of sunlight.

mcqs.q: How many colours are there in the spectrum of white light?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is seven: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. Each colour is linked to a particular frequency and wavelength. White light splits into exactly these seven colours when it passes through a prism.

mcqs.q: In each water drop of a rainbow, the sunlight undergoes:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is refraction, reflection inside the drop, and dispersion. The light first refracts as it enters the drop, reflects inside it, and disperses into seven colours. This combined action of many drops produces the rainbow seen in the sky after rain.

mcqs.q: Light from a luminous body spreads:
options: In straight lines in all directions
In curved lines in one direction
mcqs.why: The correct answer is in straight lines in all directions. Light travels outwards from a luminous body such as the Sun, a bulb or a candle along straight paths. This rectilinear propagation is a basic property of light used throughout geometrical optics.

mcqs.q: The colours separate in a prism because each colour has a different:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is wavelength and frequency. Because of this difference, each colour bends through a different angle inside the prism. In vacuum, however, all colours travel at the same speed; it is inside the prism that their behaviour differs.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Waves and the Spectrum
lessons.notes_html:
What are Electromagnetic Waves?

These are waves made up of changing electric and magnetic fields which travel even in a vacuum, without any medium, at a speed of 3 × 10^8 m/s. Light, radio waves and X-rays all belong to the same family. All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum; they differ only in frequency and wavelength.

Order of the Spectrum (in decreasing wavelength)

WaveProperty / Note
Radio wavesLongest wavelength, lowest frequency
MicrowavesRadar, ovens, satellites
InfraredHeat rays
Visible lightSeven colours
Ultraviolet (UV)Comes from the Sun, harms the skin
X-raysSeeing inside the body
Gamma raysShortest wavelength, greatest energy

Rule to remember: as the wavelength decreases, the frequency and the energy increase (v = f λ, and v is the same for all of them).

Worked Example 1

An electromagnetic wave has a wavelength of 0.15 μm. Find its frequency (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s).

λ = 0.15 μm = 0.15 × 10^-6 m = 1.5 × 10^-7 m

f = c / λ = (3 × 10^8) / (1.5 × 10^-7) = 2 × 10^15 Hz (infrared)

Worked Example 2

Green light has a wavelength of 5.5 × 10^-7 m. Find its frequency.

f = c / λ = (3 × 10^8) / (5.5 × 10^-7) = 5.45 × 10^14 Hz

mcqs.q: Electromagnetic waves are made up of changing:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is electric and magnetic fields. These changing fields travel even in a vacuum, without any medium, at a speed of 3 x 10^8 m/s. Light, radio waves and X-rays all belong to this same family of waves.

mcqs.q: All electromagnetic waves in a vacuum travel at:
options: A speed depending on colour only
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the same speed, 3 x 10^8 m/s. The members of the electromagnetic family differ only in frequency and wavelength, not in their speed in a vacuum. This is why the relation v = f lambda holds for all of them with the same v.

mcqs.q: Which member of the spectrum has the longest wavelength?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is radio waves, which have the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency in the spectrum. At the other extreme, gamma rays have the shortest wavelength. The order in decreasing wavelength is: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

mcqs.q: Which member of the spectrum has the shortest wavelength and the greatest energy?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is gamma rays. They have the shortest wavelength, and as wavelength decreases the frequency and energy increase. Radio waves are at the opposite end, with the longest wavelength and the lowest energy.

mcqs.q: As the wavelength of an electromagnetic wave decreases, its frequency and energy:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they increase. Since v = f lambda and v is the same for all electromagnetic waves, a smaller wavelength must mean a larger frequency. The energy also increases as the frequency increases, which is why gamma rays are so energetic.

mcqs.q: Microwaves are used in:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is radar, ovens and satellites, as listed in the spectrum table in the notes. Microwaves sit between radio waves and infrared in wavelength. Seeing inside the body belongs to X-rays, and treating cancer belongs to gamma rays.

mcqs.q: The infrared part of the spectrum is associated with:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is heat rays. Infrared radiation is the part of the spectrum felt as heat, lying just beyond red light. Ultraviolet, not infrared, is the part that comes from the Sun and harms the skin.

mcqs.q: An electromagnetic wave has wavelength 1.5 x 10^-7 m. Its frequency (c = 3 x 10^8 m/s) is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2 x 10^15 Hz. Using f = c / lambda = (3 x 10^8) / (1.5 x 10^-7) = 2 x 10^15 Hz. This is the first worked example in the notes, and the wave lies in the infrared region according to the notes.

mcqs.q: Green light has wavelength 5.5 x 10^-7 m. Its frequency is about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 5.45 x 10^14 Hz. From f = c / lambda = (3 x 10^8) / (5.5 x 10^-7) = 5.45 x 10^14 Hz. This is the second worked example in the notes, showing that visible light has a very high frequency.

mcqs.q: Ultraviolet rays in the spectrum are noted in the table as:
options: Coming from the Sun and harming the skin
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they come from the Sun and harm the skin. Ultraviolet lies between visible light and X-rays in the spectrum. Radar and ovens use microwaves instead, while the longest wavelength belongs to radio waves.

lessons.title: Uses and Hazards of the Parts of the Spectrum
lessons.notes_html:
Radio Waves

  • Sources — transmitters of radio and TV stations, oscillating charges
  • Uses — broadcasting and communication; because of their large wavelength they reach far away

Microwaves

  • Important in satellite communication, because they pass through the ionosphere
  • Used in radar and in microwave ovens

Infrared

  • Every warm body gives out infrared rays; they are produced by the vibration of molecules
  • At night, security staff take pictures of warm bodies with thermal cameras
  • Infrared is used in TV remote controls

Ultraviolet (UV)

  • The UV rays of the Sun burn the skin and cause damage; too much exposure is dangerous
  • A sunbed also gives out UV, so it is used under supervision

X-Rays

  • Used to find cracks in iron and in welding
  • In medicine, for pictures of bones

Gamma Rays

  • Used in radiotherapy and radiosurgery to kill cancer cells
  • Also used in medical imaging
  • Great care is essential because of their high energy

Optical Fibre

Advantages of optical fibres in communication: high-speed data with low loss, greater capacity, and protection from electrical interference. They are also used in medical and industrial work (details in Unit 13).

mcqs.q: Radio waves are used for broadcasting and communication because:
options: Their large wavelength lets them reach far away
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that their large wavelength lets them reach far away. Radio waves come from transmitters of radio and TV stations and from oscillating charges. Their long wavelength helps them travel over long distances, which makes them ideal for broadcasting.

mcqs.q: Microwaves are important in satellite communication because they:
options: Travel at half the speed of light
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they pass through the ionosphere, so they can reach satellites. Microwaves are also used in radar and in microwave ovens. Radio waves of longer wavelength would be reflected or absorbed before reaching a satellite.

mcqs.q: Every warm body gives out:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is infrared rays, which are produced by the vibration of molecules. Because warm bodies emit them, security staff at night can take pictures of warm bodies with thermal cameras. Infrared is also used in TV remote controls.

mcqs.q: Infrared rays are used in:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is TV remote controls. The remote sends infrared signals to the television. Infrared is also used in thermal cameras at night, because every warm body gives out these rays.

mcqs.q: Too much exposure to ultraviolet rays is dangerous because they:
options: Burn the skin and cause damage
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they burn the skin and cause damage. The UV rays of the Sun are the main source of this exposure. A sunbed also gives out UV, so it is used only under supervision.

mcqs.q: X-rays are used to:
options: Find cracks in iron and welding, and take pictures of bones
mcqs.why: The correct answer is finding cracks in iron and in welding, and in medicine for pictures of bones. X-rays can pass through soft material but are stopped more by dense material, which makes both uses possible. Radiotherapy uses gamma rays, not X-rays.

mcqs.q: Gamma rays are used in medicine to:
options: Kill cancer cells in radiotherapy and radiosurgery
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to kill cancer cells in radiotherapy and radiosurgery, and they are also used in medical imaging. Great care is essential because of their high energy. Their penetrating power, harmful to healthy tissue, is exactly what destroys the cancer cells.

mcqs.q: A sunbed is used under supervision because it gives out:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is ultraviolet rays. A sunbed gives out UV just like the Sun, and too much exposure burns the skin and causes damage. That is why its use is supervised rather than free.

mcqs.q: An advantage of optical fibres in communication is:
options: High-speed data with low loss and greater capacity
mcqs.why: The correct answer is high-speed data with low loss, greater capacity, and protection from electrical interference. Optical fibres are also used in medical and industrial work. These advantages make them better than ordinary wires for communication.

mcqs.q: Infrared rays are produced by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the vibration of molecules in a warm body. Every warm body gives out infrared rays for this reason. Radio waves, by contrast, are produced by transmitters and oscillating charges at radio and TV stations.

lessons.title: Reflection of Light and Mirrors
lessons.notes_html:
What is Reflection?

Reflection is the return of light into the same medium after striking a surface.

Terms of Reflection

TermMeaning
NormalThe perpendicular line to the surface at the point of incidence
Incident RayThe light coming towards the surface
Reflected RayThe light going back after striking the surface

Laws of Reflection

  • The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r)
  • The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane

Image in a Plane Mirror

  • The image is virtual, erect and of the same size as the object
  • The image forms as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it
  • The size of the image depends on the size of the object

Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors

MirrorUse and Reason
ConvexCar rear-view mirror — gives a wide field of view and an erect, diminished image
ConcaveTorch and searchlight reflector — sends the rays out as a parallel beam; a dentist also uses it to see an enlarged image of the teeth

Mirror Formula

1/f = 1/p + 1/q

Worked Example

A thin pin is placed 15 cm in front of a mirror of focal length 20 cm (f). Find the position of the image.

1/q = 1/f − 1/p — calculating with the book's sign convention, the image forms virtual behind the mirror

Note: In mirror problems the sign convention must be kept in mind; for a concave mirror f is taken as negative.

mcqs.q: In the law of reflection, the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are always:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they are always equal. In symbols, angle i = angle r, where both angles are measured from the normal. This law holds for reflection from both plane and spherical mirrors.

mcqs.q: A ray of light passing without deviation is the one that strikes the mirror:
options: At the edge of the mirror
Perpendicular to the surface, along the normal
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the ray that passes along the normal, perpendicular to the mirror. It strikes the mirror at an angle of incidence of 0 degrees and returns along the same path. Every other ray is reflected at an angle equal to its angle of incidence.

mcqs.q: The image formed by a plane mirror is always:
options: Virtual, erect and the same size
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the image is virtual, erect and the same size as the object, and it lies behind the mirror. It cannot be formed on a screen, because it is virtual. This is the standard image of the plane mirror given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Spherical mirrors are mirrors shaped as:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is parts of spheres. A spherical mirror is a hollow, polished part of a sphere. It has two types: the concave mirror and the convex mirror, depending on which side is polished.

mcqs.q: A concave mirror is also called a converging mirror because it:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it brings (converges) the rays together. A concave mirror is silvered on the inner, concave side of the hollow sphere. Parallel rays reflected by it meet at a point, which is why it is called a converging mirror.

mcqs.q: A convex mirror is silvered on the:
options: Outer side of the hollow sphere
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the outer side of the hollow sphere. Because of its bulging shape, a convex mirror spreads the reflected rays apart, so it is called a diverging mirror. It always gives a virtual, erect and diminished image.

mcqs.q: Parallel rays reflected by a concave mirror meet at the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the principal focus of the mirror. This is the defining property used in drawing ray diagrams for concave mirrors. A ray passing through the centre of curvature, by contrast, strikes the mirror perpendicularly and returns along its own path.

mcqs.q: A ray of light passing through the centre of curvature of a spherical mirror:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it returns along the same path. Such a ray strikes the mirror perpendicularly along the normal, so its angle of incidence is zero. This is one of the standard rules for drawing ray diagrams with spherical mirrors.

mcqs.q: When you stand in front of a plane mirror, the image is:
options: On the surface of the mirror
Behind the mirror, the same size as you
mcqs.why: The correct answer is behind the mirror and the same size as the object. The plane mirror always forms a virtual, erect image of the same size. It appears behind the mirror even though the reflected rays never actually go there.

mcqs.q: A convex mirror is called a diverging mirror because the reflected rays:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the reflected rays spread apart (diverge). This is the opposite of the concave mirror, which converges the rays. Because the rays diverge, a convex mirror covers a wider field of view.

lessons.title: Refraction of Light and Refractive Index
lessons.notes_html:
What is Refraction?

Refraction is the bending of light from its path when it enters from one medium into another. The reason is that the speed of light is different in every medium.

  • From a denser medium to a rarer medium: the ray bends away from the normal
  • From a rarer medium to a denser medium: the ray bends towards the normal

Laws of Refraction

  • The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal all lie in the same plane
  • sin i / sin r = constant (Snell's Law)

Refractive Index (n)

n = c / v = sin i / sin r

  • The refractive index of water is n = 1.33 and of diamond is n = 2.41
  • The greater the value of n, the slower light travels in that medium and the more it bends
  • Refraction depends on these factors: the nature of the two media and the wavelength of the light

Glass Slab

Passing through a slab, the ray bends at both parallel surfaces and the emerging ray remains parallel to the incident ray, only shifted slightly sideways (lateral shift). The refractive index can be measured by the slab experiment: n = real depth / apparent depth is also related to it.

Worked Example

Light enters water from air. The angle of incidence is 40° and n for water = 1.33. Find the angle of refraction.

n = sin i / sin r → sin r = sin 40° / 1.33 = 0.643 / 1.33 = 0.483

r = sin^-1 (0.483) = 28.9°

The ray bends towards the normal in the denser medium, so r is smaller than i.

mcqs.q: Refraction is the bending of light when it:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is when light enters a different medium obliquely. In refraction the speed and wavelength of light change, but the frequency stays the same. A ray entering along the normal is the exception: it passes straight without bending.

mcqs.q: When light enters a denser medium, it:
options: Does not bend at any angle
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it bends towards the normal, and it also slows down. The bending happens because the speed of light decreases in the denser medium. On entering a rarer medium, the light speeds up and bends away from the normal instead.

mcqs.q: The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in a medium is called the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the refractive index, n = c / v. It is a measure of how much the light slows down in that medium. A larger refractive index means a slower speed and a greater bending of the light.

mcqs.q: The refractive index of water is 1.33, so the speed of light in water is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2.25 x 10^8 m/s. From n = c / v, v = c / n = (3 x 10^8) / 1.33 = 2.25 x 10^8 m/s. This is the worked example on refractive index given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Light of frequency 5 x 10^14 Hz and speed 3 x 10^8 m/s in air enters glass of refractive index 1.52. In the glass, its speed and frequency are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is speed 1.97 x 10^8 m/s and frequency 5 x 10^14 Hz. The speed in glass is v = c / n = (3 x 10^8) / 1.52 = 1.97 x 10^8 m/s, while the frequency stays unchanged in refraction. This is the second worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is because of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is refraction. Light from the bottom of the pool bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, so the bottom appears raised. The same effect makes a pencil in water look bent, as shown in the notes' figure.

mcqs.q: When light passes from a denser medium to a rarer medium, it:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it bends away from the normal, and its speed increases. This is the reverse of entering a denser medium, where light slows down and bends towards the normal. The amount of bending grows as the angle of incidence increases.

mcqs.q: In refraction, the quantity that remains unchanged is the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is frequency. The speed and the wavelength both change when light enters a new medium, and the direction changes too unless the ray is along the normal. The frequency is fixed by the source and never changes in refraction.

mcqs.q: Light bends in refraction because:
options: Its speed changes in the new medium
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that its speed changes in the new medium. Light is slower in a denser medium and faster in a rarer one, and this change of speed at the boundary bends the ray. The frequency, however, remains the same throughout.

mcqs.q: The refractive index of glass used in the notes' example is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 1.52. In the worked example, light entering glass of refractive index 1.52 slows down to 1.97 x 10^8 m/s. Water's refractive index in the other example is 1.33, and 1.00 would mean the speed is unchanged, as in vacuum.

lessons.title: Total Internal Reflection and Optical Fibre
lessons.notes_html:
Critical Angle

The angle of incidence in the denser medium at which the angle of refraction becomes 90° is the critical angle.

sin C = 1 / n

  • The critical angle for water is about 48.8° (n = 1.33)
  • For diamond it is 24.5° (n = 2.41) — this small critical angle is the reason for the sparkle of diamond

Worked Example

Find the critical angle of diamond (n = 2.41).

sin C = 1 / 2.41 = 0.415

C = sin^-1 (0.415) = 24.5°

Total Internal Reflection

When light coming from a denser medium strikes the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, it is reflected completely back into the same medium instead of passing into the second medium.

Conditions

  • Light must go from a denser medium towards a rarer medium
  • The angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle

Everyday Examples and Uses

  • The sparkle of diamond, water appearing on the road on a hot day (mirage)
  • Optical fibre: the inner part (core) has a higher refractive index and the outer layer (cladding) has a lower one; light travels forward inside by continuous total internal reflection
  • Endoscope: the doctor sees the inner parts of the body through the fibre

mcqs.q: The critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 90 degrees: at the critical angle, the refracted ray just grazes the boundary. For any angle of incidence greater than this, total internal reflection takes place instead of refraction. The critical angle depends on the refractive index of the medium.

mcqs.q: Total internal reflection takes place when light in a denser medium strikes the boundary at an angle:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is greater than the critical angle. The light is then reflected completely back into the denser medium, with no refraction into the rarer medium. Two conditions are needed: light must be in the denser medium, and the angle must exceed the critical angle.

mcqs.q: The relation between the refractive index and the critical angle C is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is n = 1 / sin C. This formula lets us find the critical angle of any medium from its refractive index. For diamond, with n = 2.42, it gives a critical angle of only about 24.5 degrees.

mcqs.q: The critical angle for diamond (n = 2.42) is about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is about 24.5 degrees. From sin C = 1 / n = 1 / 2.42 = 0.4132, C = sin^-1(0.4132) = 24.4 degrees, about 24.5 degrees. This very small critical angle is why a cut diamond sparkles so strongly, as the notes explain.

mcqs.q: A diamond sparkles because of:
options: Reflection from its outer surface only
Total internal reflection and its small critical angle
mcqs.why: The correct answer is total internal reflection together with its small critical angle of about 24.5 degrees. Light entering a diamond is reflected again and again inside it before coming out. This trapped light, escaping from the top, gives the diamond its sparkle.

mcqs.q: A periscope works on the principle of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is total internal reflection using two right-angled prisms. Each prism turns the light through 90 degrees, so the observer can see over an obstacle. The same principle is used in binoculars and in SLR cameras.

mcqs.q: In optical fibres, information is carried by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is light undergoing total internal reflection. The light travels inside the thin glass fibre, reflecting again and again from its walls without escaping. This is how data is transmitted quickly over long distances in communication.

mcqs.q: For total internal reflection, the light must be travelling:
options: From a denser to a rarer medium
From a rarer to a denser medium
mcqs.why: The correct answer is from a denser medium to a rarer medium. If light were going from rarer to denser, it would bend towards the normal and always pass through; total internal reflection could never occur. The angle of incidence must also be greater than the critical angle.

mcqs.q: When the angle of incidence equals the critical angle, the refracted ray:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the refracted ray grazes along the boundary, at 90 degrees to the normal. This borderline case defines the critical angle itself. Increasing the angle of incidence beyond this point gives total internal reflection.

mcqs.q: Which of these does NOT use total internal reflection, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the plane mirror, which works by ordinary reflection from its silvered surface. Optical fibres, periscopes, binoculars and SLR cameras all use prisms or fibres based on total internal reflection. The sparkling of a cut diamond is also due to this effect.

lessons.title: Lenses and Optical Instruments
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Lens?

A lens is a piece of transparent material (glass/plastic) with at least one curved surface. A lens forms images by the refraction of light.

Convex LensConcave Lens
Thick in the middle, converges the rays (converging)Thin in the middle, diverges the rays (diverging)
Can form a real imageAlways forms a virtual, erect, diminished image

Lens Formulas

1/f = 1/p + 1/q    and    P = 1 / f (f in metres; the unit of P is the dioptre, D)

Worked Example

An object is placed 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the position of the image.

1/q = 1/f − 1/p = 1/10 − 1/15 = (3 − 2)/30 = 1/30

q = 30 cm — the image forms real and inverted at 30 cm on the other side

Magnifying Glass

When a convex lens is held at a distance less than one focal length from the object, a magnified, erect and virtual image is formed. It is also called a simple microscope. It does not form a real and inverted image.

Optical Instruments

InstrumentConstruction / Use
Simple MicroscopeOne convex lens; magnifying glass
Compound MicroscopeTwo lenses: objective (small f) and eyepiece (large f); to see very small objects magnified
TelescopeFor stars and distant objects; a telescope is used to see stars in dim light

mcqs.q: A lens forms images by the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is refraction of light. A lens is a piece of transparent material such as glass or plastic with at least one curved surface, and it bends light as the light passes through it. Mirrors, by contrast, form images by reflection.

mcqs.q: A convex lens is:
options: Thick in the middle and converging
Thin in the middle and diverging
mcqs.why: The correct answer is thick in the middle, and it converges the rays passing through it, so it is called a converging lens. It can form a real image. A concave lens is thin in the middle and diverges the rays.

mcqs.q: A concave lens always forms an image that is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is virtual, erect and diminished. Because a concave lens diverges the rays, they never meet to form a real image on the other side. This is true for an object at any distance from a concave lens.

mcqs.q: The power of a lens is given by P = 1 / f, where f is in metres. The unit of power is the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the dioptre, symbol D. The focal length must be expressed in metres when using P = 1 / f; using centimetres would give a wrong value. A shorter focal length means a greater power.

mcqs.q: An object is placed 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. The image forms at:
options: 30 cm on the other side, real and inverted
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 30 cm on the other side, real and inverted. From 1/q = 1/f - 1/p = 1/10 - 1/15 = 1/30, so q = 30 cm, as worked out in the notes. Because the image distance is positive and the image is on the other side, it is real.

mcqs.q: A magnifying glass is a convex lens used with the object placed:
options: Exactly at the focal point only
At a distance less than one focal length
mcqs.why: The correct answer is at a distance less than one focal length from the lens. A magnified, erect and virtual image is then formed, which is why the magnifying glass is also called a simple microscope. It does not form a real and inverted image.

mcqs.q: A compound microscope uses:
options: Two lenses: an objective of small f and an eyepiece of large f
A lens and a mirror only
mcqs.why: The correct answer is two lenses: an objective with a small focal length and an eyepiece with a large focal length. Together they magnify very small objects much more than a single lens can. A simple microscope, in contrast, has only one convex lens.

mcqs.q: A telescope is an optical instrument used for:
options: Examining the inside of the body
mcqs.why: The correct answer is seeing stars and distant objects; a telescope is used to see stars in dim light. Very small objects are the job of the microscope. The endoscope, a different instrument again, is used inside the body.

mcqs.q: If a convex lens has focal length 0.25 m, its power is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 4 D. Using P = 1 / f with f in metres gives P = 1 / 0.25 = 4 dioptres. Remember that the focal length must be in metres for this formula, not in centimetres.

mcqs.q: The simple microscope is another name for:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the magnifying glass, which is a single convex lens. Held within one focal length of the object, it gives a magnified, erect and virtual image. The compound microscope is a separate instrument with two lenses.

lessons.title: The Human Eye and Eye Defects
lessons.notes_html:
The Human Eye

The eye is a natural camera. Its lens refracts light and forms a real and inverted image on the retina. A normal eye can see objects clearly from 25 cm (the near point) to far away; objects closer than this are not seen clearly.

Two Main Defects of the Eye

DefectCause / Where the Image FormsCorrection
Short Sight (Myopia)Distant objects appear blurred; the image forms in front of the retinaConcave lens
Long Sight (Hyperopia)Near objects appear blurred; the image forms behind the retinaConvex lens

In short sight, lengthening of the eyeball or excessive bending by the lens brings the image forward; a concave lens diverges the rays a little and takes the image onto the retina. In long sight the opposite happens and a convex lens helps by converging the rays beforehand.

mcqs.q: In the human eye, the image formed on the retina is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is real and inverted. The eye is a natural camera: its lens refracts light and forms the image on the retina at the back of the eye. The brain then interprets this inverted image correctly.

mcqs.q: A normal eye can see objects clearly from the near point, which is at:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 25 cm. A normal eye sees clearly from 25 cm to far away; objects closer than 25 cm are not seen clearly. This nearest clear distance is called the near point of the eye.

mcqs.q: In short sight (myopia), the image forms:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is in front of the retina, so distant objects appear blurred. This happens because of the lengthening of the eyeball or excessive bending by the lens. A concave lens is used to correct it.

mcqs.q: Short sight (myopia) is corrected by using a:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a concave lens. It diverges the incoming rays a little, so the image is pushed back onto the retina instead of forming in front of it. A convex lens would bend the rays even more and make the defect worse.

mcqs.q: In long sight (hyperopia), the image forms:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is behind the retina, so near objects appear blurred. A convex lens corrects this defect by converging the rays beforehand. Long sight is therefore the opposite defect to short sight.

mcqs.q: Long sight (hyperopia) is corrected by using a:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a convex lens. It converges the rays before they enter the eye, so the eye lens can bring the image forward onto the retina. In long sight the image would otherwise form behind the retina.

mcqs.q: A person who cannot see distant objects clearly, but sees near objects well, has:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is short sight, or myopia. In this defect distant objects appear blurred because their image forms in front of the retina. It is corrected with a concave lens in spectacles.

mcqs.q: A person who cannot see near objects clearly has:
options: Short sight corrected by a convex lens
mcqs.why: The correct answer is long sight, or hyperopia. Near objects appear blurred because the image forms behind the retina. A convex lens, which converges the rays beforehand, is used to correct it.

mcqs.q: One cause of short sight given in the notes is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the lengthening of the eyeball; excessive bending by the eye lens is the other cause given. Both make the image form in front of the retina. A concave lens then diverges the rays slightly and takes the image back onto the retina.

mcqs.q: Objects closer than 25 cm are not seen clearly by a normal eye because 25 cm is its:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the near point. A normal eye can focus clearly from the near point at 25 cm all the way to distant objects. Anything brought closer than this distance cannot be focused sharply on the retina.

lessons.title: Electric Charge and Electroscope
lessons.notes_html:
Electrostatics

The branch of physics in which static electric charge is studied is called electrostatics.

Types of Charge

  • Positive charge (+) and negative charge (−)
  • Like charges repel each other; opposite charges attract each other
  • The unit of charge is the coulomb (C); 1 C is a very large charge

Simple Experiments

Rubbing a glass rod with silk gives it a positive charge, and rubbing an ebonite rod with fur gives it a negative charge. A charged rod attracts light bits of paper, which shows the presence of charge.

Electroscope

This instrument is used to detect the presence and type of charge on a body.

  • Construction — a metal rod, a knob at the top and two thin gold leaves at the bottom
  • On touching or bringing a charged body near the knob, both leaves take the same charge and open apart by repelling each other
  • The greater the opening of the leaves, the greater the charge

mcqs.q: The branch of physics that studies static electric charge is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is electrostatics. It deals with charges at rest, their attraction and repulsion, and instruments such as the electroscope. Current electricity, by contrast, studies charges in motion.

mcqs.q: Like charges ______ each other, and opposite charges ______ each other.
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: like charges repel and opposite charges attract. Two positive charges, or two negative charges, push each other away, while a positive and a negative charge pull together. This is a basic rule of electrostatics.

mcqs.q: The unit of electric charge is the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the coulomb, symbol C. One coulomb is a very large charge; the charges in these experiments are usually tiny fractions of a coulomb. The ampere is the unit of current and the volt of potential difference.

mcqs.q: Rubbing a glass rod with silk gives the rod a:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a positive charge. Rubbing an ebonite rod with fur, on the other hand, gives it a negative charge. These simple experiments are used to produce the two types of charge for electrostatic demonstrations.

mcqs.q: Rubbing an ebonite rod with fur gives the rod a:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a negative charge. The glass rod rubbed with silk becomes positive, while ebonite rubbed with fur becomes negative. A charged rod of either kind attracts light bits of paper, which shows the presence of charge.

mcqs.q: An electroscope is an instrument used to:
options: Detect the presence and type of charge on a body
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to detect the presence and type of charge on a body. It has a metal rod with a knob at the top and two thin gold leaves at the bottom. The behaviour of the leaves shows whether a body is charged and what kind of charge it carries.

mcqs.q: When a charged body is brought near the knob of an electroscope, the two gold leaves:
options: Take the same charge and open apart by repelling each other
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that both leaves take the same charge and open apart by repelling each other, because like charges repel. The greater the opening of the leaves, the greater the charge. If there were no charge, the leaves would hang together.

mcqs.q: In an electroscope, a greater opening of the leaves shows:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a greater charge. The leaves repel each other more strongly when they carry more of the same charge, so they open wider. The electroscope thus gives a rough comparison of amounts of charge as well as detecting it.

mcqs.q: A charged rod attracts light bits of paper. This shows:
options: The presence of charge on the rod
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it shows the presence of charge on the rod. Attraction of light objects is a simple test for a charged body used in electrostatics. An uncharged rod would leave the bits of paper undisturbed.

mcqs.q: The two types of electric charge are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is positive (+) and negative (-). Every charged body carries one of these two kinds of charge. Like charges repel each other and opposite charges attract, which is the foundation of all electrostatic effects.

lessons.title: Coulomb's Law and Electric Field
lessons.notes_html:
Coulomb's Law

The force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

F = k q1 q2 / r^2,   k = 9 × 10^9 N m^2 C^-2

This law resembles Newton's law of gravitation — in both, the force decreases with the square of the distance.

Worked Example 1

Two charges q1 = 5 μC and q2 = 3 μC are 5 cm apart. Find the force.

q1 = 5 × 10^-6 C, q2 = 3 × 10^-6 C, r = 0.05 m

F = (9 × 10^9 × 5 × 10^-6 × 3 × 10^-6) / (0.05)^2 = (9 × 10^9 × 15 × 10^-12) / 0.0025 = 54 N

Worked Example 2

Find the force between two electrons at a distance of 1 m (e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C).

F = 9 × 10^9 × (1.6 × 10^-19)^2 / 1^2 = 2.3 × 10^-28 N

Note: At the same distance, the force between two protons will also be the same, because the charge is the same.

Electric Field and Its Intensity

The region around a charge where another charge feels a force is the electric field. The intensity of the field is the force on a unit positive charge:

E = F / q,   unit: N/C

Worked Example 3

The field intensity on a 2 μC charge is 3.42 × 10^11 N/C. Find the force.

F = E × q = 3.42 × 10^11 × 2 × 10^-6 = 6.84 × 10^5 N

Field lines go from a positive charge towards a negative charge. A charged particle moves in the field along the direction of the lines (a positive particle) or in the opposite direction (a negative particle).

mcqs.q: According to Coulomb's law, the force between two point charges is inversely proportional to:
options: The square of the distance between them
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the square of the distance between them, F = k q1 q2 / r^2. The force is directly proportional to the product of the charges. This law resembles Newton's law of gravitation, because in both the force decreases with the square of the distance.

mcqs.q: In Coulomb's law F = k q1 q2 / r^2, the value of k is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2. This large constant is used in every Coulomb's law calculation in the notes. The value 1.6 x 10^-19 C is the charge on one electron, a different quantity altogether.

mcqs.q: Two charges of 5 microC and 3 microC are 5 cm apart. The force between them is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 54 N. Using F = (9 x 10^9 x 5 x 10^-6 x 3 x 10^-6) / (0.05)^2 = (9 x 10^9 x 15 x 10^-12) / 0.0025 = 54 N. This is the first worked example of Coulomb's law in the notes.

mcqs.q: The force between two electrons 1 m apart (e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C) is about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2.3 x 10^-28 N. From F = 9 x 10^9 x (1.6 x 10^-19)^2 / 1^2, the force is extremely small because the charge on an electron is tiny. At the same distance, the force between two protons would be the same, because the charge is the same.

mcqs.q: At the same distance, the force between two protons equals that between two electrons because:
options: The magnitude of their charge is the same
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the magnitude of their charge is the same, 1.6 x 10^-19 C. Coulomb's law depends on the charges and the distance, not on the masses. So equal charges at equal distances always give equal forces.

mcqs.q: The electric field around a charge is the region where:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is where another charge feels a force. The intensity of the field at a point is the force on a unit positive charge placed there, E = F / q. Its unit is the newton per coulomb (N/C).

mcqs.q: The unit of electric field intensity is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is N/C, newton per coulomb, because E = F / q is a force divided by a charge. Field intensity tells how strong the field is at a point. A larger value means a stronger push on any charge placed there.

mcqs.q: The field intensity on a 2 microC charge is 3.42 x 10^11 N/C. The force on it is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 6.84 x 10^5 N. From F = E x q = 3.42 x 10^11 x 2 x 10^-6 = 6.84 x 10^5 N. This is the third worked example in the notes on Coulomb's law and electric field.

mcqs.q: Electric field lines go:
options: From a positive charge towards a negative charge
From a negative charge towards a positive charge
mcqs.why: The correct answer is from a positive charge towards a negative charge. A positive particle placed in the field moves along the direction of the lines, while a negative particle moves in the opposite direction. The lines therefore show the direction of the force on a positive charge.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two charges is doubled, the force between them becomes:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is one quarter. Coulomb's law has r^2 in the denominator, so doubling r divides the force by 2^2 = 4. This inverse-square behaviour is the same as in Newton's law of gravitation, which the notes compare it with.

lessons.title: Electric Potential and Potential Difference
lessons.notes_html:
Electric Potential

The work done in bringing a unit positive charge to a point is the electric potential at that point.

V = W / q,   unit: volt (V)

Potential Difference

The work done in moving a unit charge between two points is called the potential difference. Charge always flows from higher potential to lower potential, and on the way its energy changes into other forms (light, heat, motion).

Worked Example

The potential difference between two points is 100 V. In moving a charge, 500 J of work is done. Find the charge.

q = W / V = 500 / 100 = 5 C

Lightning and Protection

Lightning is a large example of electrostatic discharge. As charge collects in the clouds, a large potential difference is produced and the charge descends to the ground with a flash.

  • A lightning conductor is fitted on buildings, which carries the charge directly into the ground
  • Standing under a tree or in an open field during lightning is dangerous

mcqs.q: The electric potential at a point is the work done in bringing to that point a:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a unit positive charge, and V = W / q. Electric potential is measured in volts. It tells how much work is needed to bring each coulomb of positive charge to that point.

mcqs.q: The unit of electric potential is the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the volt, symbol V. Potential and potential difference are both measured in volts, since V = W / q is work in joules divided by charge in coulombs. One volt is one joule per coulomb.

mcqs.q: Potential difference between two points is the work done in:
options: Moving a unit charge between the two points
mcqs.why: The correct answer is moving a unit charge between the two points. Charge always flows from higher potential to lower potential, and on the way its energy changes into other forms such as light, heat and motion. This energy change is what makes circuits useful.

mcqs.q: Charge in a conductor always flows from:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is from higher potential to lower potential. As the charge flows, its electrical energy changes into other forms like light, heat and motion. A battery's job in a circuit is to maintain this potential difference.

mcqs.q: The potential difference between two points is 100 V and 500 J of work is done in moving a charge. The charge is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 5 C. From q = W / V = 500 / 100 = 5 C, using V = W / q rearranged. This is the worked example given in the notes for electric potential.

mcqs.q: If V = W / q, then a potential difference of 100 V with a charge of 5 C means the work done is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 500 J, because W = V x q = 100 x 5 = 500 J. This is the reverse of the worked example in the notes, where 500 J and 100 V gave a charge of 5 C. The three quantities V, W and q are linked by this one relation.

mcqs.q: Lightning is a large example of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is electrostatic discharge. As charge collects in the clouds, a large potential difference is produced and the charge descends to the ground with a flash. It is the biggest natural demonstration of static electricity discharging.

mcqs.q: A lightning conductor fitted on a building protects it by:
options: Carrying the charge directly into the ground
Storing the charge in a capacitor
mcqs.why: The correct answer is carrying the charge directly into the ground, giving it a safe path so the building is not damaged. Standing under a tree or in an open field during lightning is dangerous. The conductor does not prevent lightning; it guides its charge safely to earth.

mcqs.q: During lightning it is dangerous to:
options: Stand under a tree or in an open field
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to stand under a tree or in an open field, because the discharge may strike through such exposed positions. A lightning conductor on a building carries the charge directly into the ground instead. Safety during thunderstorms is an application of electrostatics from these notes.

mcqs.q: As charge flows from higher to lower potential, its energy changes into:
options: Other forms such as light, heat and motion
mcqs.why: The correct answer is other forms such as light, heat and motion. This is why a bulb glows and a motor turns when charge flows through them. Energy is never lost; the electrical energy is simply converted.

lessons.title: Capacitor
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Capacitor?

A capacitor is a device that stores electric charge and energy. It is made of two metal plates with an insulating material (dielectric) between them.

Capacitance

C = Q / V,   unit: farad (F); μF is commonly used

Worked Example 1

The potential difference across a 40 μF capacitor is 6 V. Find the stored charge.

Q = C × V = 40 × 6 = 240 μC

Factors Affecting Capacitance

  • Increasing the area of the plates increases the capacitance
  • Decreasing the distance between the plates increases the capacitance
  • Placing a dielectric between the plates increases the capacitance

Combinations of Capacitors

SeriesParallel
1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + …, the capacitance decreasesC = C1 + C2 + …, the capacitance increases
The charge on each capacitor is the sameThe voltage across each capacitor is the same

Worked Example 2

Capacitors of 2 μF, 3 μF and 4 μF are joined in series. Find the equivalent capacitance.

1/C = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 = (6 + 4 + 3)/12 = 13/12

C = 12/13 = 0.92 μF

If two 8 μF capacitors are joined in series, the equivalent capacitance will be 4 μF; in parallel it will be 16 μF.

Uses
