Capacitors are used in the tuning of radios and TVs, in a camera flash, in starting fans and motors, and in smoothing the power supply. Finding the equivalent capacitance is necessary so that capacitors can be joined in the correct way to obtain the required capacitance.

mcqs.q: A capacitor is a device that stores:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is electric charge and energy. A capacitor is made of two metal plates with an insulating material, called a dielectric, between them. Its ability to store charge is measured by its capacitance.

mcqs.q: A capacitor is made of:
options: Two metal plates with a dielectric between them
mcqs.why: The correct answer is two metal plates with an insulating material (dielectric) between them. Charge collects on the plates when a potential difference is applied. The capacitance is C = Q / V, measured in farads.

mcqs.q: Capacitance is defined as C = Q / V. Its unit is the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the farad, symbol F; in practice the microfarad (uF) is commonly used because the farad is very large. Capacitance tells how much charge is stored for each volt applied. It is increased by bigger plates, smaller separation, or a dielectric.

mcqs.q: The potential difference across a 40 uF capacitor is 6 V. The stored charge is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 240 uC. From Q = C x V = 40 x 6 = 240 uC. This is the first worked example in the notes on capacitors, using C = Q / V rearranged.

mcqs.q: Which change increases the capacitance of a capacitor?
options: Decreasing the area of the plates
Increasing the distance between the plates
Increasing the area of the plates
mcqs.why: The correct answer is increasing the area of the plates. Capacitance also increases when the distance between the plates is decreased, and when a dielectric is placed between the plates. All three factors are listed in the notes as ways to increase capacitance.

mcqs.q: Placing a dielectric between the plates of a capacitor:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it increases the capacitance. A dielectric is an insulating material, and every capacitor is built with one between its plates. Together with larger plate area and smaller plate distance, it raises the charge stored per volt.

mcqs.q: When capacitors are joined in series, the equivalent capacitance:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it decreases; the combination follows 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ... In series the charge on each capacitor is the same. Joining in parallel does the opposite and increases the capacitance.

mcqs.q: When capacitors are joined in parallel, the equivalent capacitance is:
options: C = C1 + C2 + ..., so it increases
mcqs.why: The correct answer is C = C1 + C2 + ..., so the capacitance increases. In parallel the voltage across each capacitor is the same, and their capacitances simply add up. This is the opposite behaviour to the series combination.

mcqs.q: Capacitors of 2 uF, 3 uF and 4 uF are joined in series. The equivalent capacitance is about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is about 0.92 uF. From 1/C = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 = 13/12, so C = 12/13 = 0.92 uF. Notice the series result is smaller than the smallest capacitor, 2 uF, which matches the rule that series joining decreases capacitance.

mcqs.q: Two 8 uF capacitors joined in series give 4 uF; joined in parallel they give:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 16 uF, because in parallel capacitances add: 8 + 8 = 16 uF. In series they give only 4 uF, as stated in the notes. Finding the equivalent capacitance is necessary so capacitors can be joined in the correct way to obtain the required value.

lessons.title: Electric Current and Potential Difference
lessons.notes_html:
Electric Current

The rate of flow of charge through a conductor is called electric current.

I = Q / t,   Unit: ampere (A)

  • Conventional Current — the direction of flow of positive charge, from higher potential to lower potential
  • In reality, electrons flow in a metal, and they move in the opposite direction to the conventional current
  • A potential difference (a battery) is essential in the circuit for current to flow — the work of the battery is to maintain a potential difference across the ends of the conductor

Worked Example 1

The current in a pocket calculator is 0.0002 A. How much charge flows in each minute?

Q = I × t = 0.0002 × 60 = 0.012 C

Worked Example 2

An electric heater uses a charge of 2100 C in 5 minutes. Find the current.

I = Q / t = 2100 / 300 = 7 A

Potential Difference and Work

V = W / q

Worked Example 3

The work done in moving a +9 μC charge from A to B is 9 × 10^-4 J. Find the potential difference between A and B.

V = W / q = (9 × 10^-4) / (9 × 10^-6) = 100 V

Ammeter and Voltmeter

InstrumentMeasuresConnection
AmmeterCurrentAlways in series
VoltmeterPotential differenceAlways in parallel

mcqs.q: Electric current is defined as:
options: The total charge in a wire
The rate of flow of charge through a conductor
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the rate of flow of charge through a conductor, I = Q / t. Its unit is the ampere (A). A current of one ampere means one coulomb of charge passes each second.

mcqs.q: The unit of electric current is the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the ampere, symbol A. Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series. The coulomb is the unit of charge, and the volt is the unit of potential difference.

mcqs.q: Conventional current is taken as the direction of flow of:
options: Positive charge, from higher to lower potential
mcqs.why: The correct answer is positive charge, flowing from higher potential to lower potential. In reality, electrons flow in a metal in the opposite direction to the conventional current. The convention was fixed before electrons were known and is still used in circuit diagrams.

mcqs.q: In a metal wire, the actual flow is of electrons, which move:
options: In the same direction as conventional current
mcqs.why: The correct answer is opposite to the conventional current. Conventional current is defined as the flow of positive charge, but metals carry current by electrons. So the electron flow and the conventional current point in opposite directions in the same wire.

mcqs.q: The current in a pocket calculator is 0.0002 A. The charge flowing in each minute is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 0.012 C. From Q = I x t = 0.0002 x 60 = 0.012 C, since one minute is 60 seconds. This is the first worked example in the notes on electric current.

mcqs.q: An electric heater uses a charge of 2100 C in 5 minutes. The current is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 7 A. From I = Q / t = 2100 / 300 = 7 A, because 5 minutes is 300 seconds. This is the second worked example in the notes, showing how current is found from charge and time.

mcqs.q: For current to flow in a circuit, the essential thing the battery provides is:
options: A potential difference across the conductor
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a potential difference across the ends of the conductor; the work of the battery is to maintain it. Without a potential difference, charge has no reason to flow. Current is the rate at which charge then moves through the conductor.

mcqs.q: The work done in moving a +9 uC charge from A to B is 9 x 10^-4 J. The potential difference between A and B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 100 V. From V = W / q = (9 x 10^-4) / (9 x 10^-6) = 100 V. This is the third worked example in the notes, using the same V = W / q relation as for electric potential.

mcqs.q: An ammeter is connected ______ and a voltmeter is connected ______ in a circuit.
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel. The ammeter measures the current passing through a part of the circuit, so the current must flow through it. The voltmeter measures the potential difference between two points, so it is joined across them.

mcqs.q: If a charge of 0.012 C flows in 60 s, the current is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 0.0002 A. From I = Q / t = 0.012 / 60 = 0.0002 A. This is the same pocket calculator example of the notes read in reverse, confirming the relation between charge, current and time.

lessons.title: Ohm's Law and Resistance
lessons.notes_html:
Ohm's Law

At constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference applied across its ends.

V = I R

  • Condition: the temperature must stay constant; the law does not apply to semiconductors
  • Increasing the voltage increases the current; increasing the resistance decreases the current

Resistance

The property of a body that opposes the flow of electric charges is called resistance. Unit: ohm (Ω).

Factors Affecting Resistance

FactorEffect
Length (L)Longer wire = more resistance (R ∝ L)
Cross-sectional area (A)Thicker wire = less resistance (R ∝ 1/A)
Nature of material (ρ)Every material has its own specific resistivity
TemperatureIn metals, resistance increases as temperature rises

R = ρ L / A

Resistance does not depend on the density of the conductor.

Worked Example

A radio's battery is 6.0 V and a current of 20 mA flows. Find the resistance of the radio.

I = 20 mA = 0.02 A

R = V / I = 6.0 / 0.02 = 300 Ω

States of a Circuit

  • Complete circuit — the path is closed and current flows
  • Open (incomplete) circuit — the path is broken, resistance is very large and current is zero
  • Short circuit — resistance is very small and current rises to a dangerous level

mcqs.q: Ohm's law states that at constant temperature, the current through a conductor is:
options: Proportional to the square of the potential difference
Inversely proportional to the potential difference
Directly proportional to the potential difference
mcqs.why: The correct answer is directly proportional to the potential difference, giving V = I R. The condition is that the temperature must stay constant. The law does not apply to semiconductors, as noted in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Ohm's law does not apply to:
options: A radio circuit at fixed temperature
mcqs.why: The correct answer is semiconductors. Ohm's law holds for conductors whose temperature stays constant, but semiconductor devices do not obey the simple V = I R relation. This limitation is stated directly in the notes.

mcqs.q: Resistance is the property of a body that:
options: Opposes the flow of electric charges
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it opposes the flow of electric charges, and its unit is the ohm. Increasing the resistance decreases the current for a given voltage. Resistance depends on length, area, material and temperature.

mcqs.q: The resistance of a wire increases when:
options: It is cooled in every case
mcqs.why: The correct answer is when its length increases, since R is proportional to L. A thicker wire has less resistance because R is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area A. These relations are combined in R = rho L / A.

mcqs.q: A thicker wire has ______ resistance because R is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area.
mcqs.why: The correct answer is less resistance. With more cross-sectional area, the charges have an easier path, so R falls as A grows. This is why thick cables are used where large currents must flow with small losses.

mcqs.q: The resistance formula R = rho L / A shows that resistance does NOT depend on:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the density of the conductor; the notes state this directly. Resistance depends on the length L, the cross-sectional area A, and the specific resistivity rho of the material. In metals it also increases as the temperature rises.

mcqs.q: In metals, as the temperature rises, the resistance:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it increases. This is one of the factors affecting resistance listed in the notes, and it is also why Ohm's law is stated for constant temperature. A hot filament, for example, has much more resistance than a cold one.

mcqs.q: A radio's battery is 6.0 V and a current of 20 mA flows. The resistance of the radio is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 300 ohm. From R = V / I = 6.0 / 0.02 = 300 ohm, since 20 mA is 0.02 A. This is the worked example of Ohm's law given in the notes.

mcqs.q: In a short circuit, the resistance is very small and the current:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it rises to a dangerous level, which is why short circuits can cause fires. In an open (incomplete) circuit the resistance is very large and the current is zero. A complete circuit has a closed path so current flows normally.

mcqs.q: In an open (incomplete) circuit:
options: The battery is damaged at once
The path is broken and current is zero
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the path is broken, the resistance is effectively very large and the current is zero. A complete circuit, with the path closed, is needed for current to flow. A short circuit is the opposite extreme, with very small resistance and dangerously large current.

lessons.title: Combinations of Resistances and Electrical Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Combinations of Resistances

SeriesParallel
R = R1 + R2 + …1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …
Current is the same, voltage is dividedVoltage is the same, current is divided
If one fails, the whole circuit stopsEach appliance can be used separately

Household appliances are joined in parallel so that each one gets the full voltage and the others keep working when one is switched off.

Worked Example

Resistances of 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 12 Ω are joined in parallel and connected to a 6 V source. Find (i) the equivalent resistance (ii) the total current (iii) the current through each resistance.

1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12 = (3 + 2 + 1)/12 = 6/12 → R = 2 Ω

Total current I = V/R = 6/2 = 3 A

Through each: 6/4 = 1.5 A, 6/6 = 1 A, 6/12 = 0.5 A (sum = 3 A ✓)

In the same way, 6 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel give R = 4 Ω.

Joule's Law and Electric Power

The heat produced in a resistance when current flows:

H = I^2 R t    and    P = V I = I^2 R = V^2 / R

The energy wasted in a resistance comes out as heat — this is useful in a heater and a bulb, but a loss in wires.

Worked Example 2

In a 220 V circuit there are 80 W and 120 W bulbs. Which has the greater resistance and through which does more current pass?

R = V^2 / P: 80 W → (220)^2/80 = 605 Ω ; 120 W → (220)^2/120 = 403 Ω

So the 80 W bulb has the greater resistance, and more current passes through the 120 W bulb (I = P/V).

mcqs.q: Resistances joined in series have equivalent resistance:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is R = R1 + R2 + ... for a series combination. In series the current is the same through each resistance while the voltage is divided between them. If one fails in series, the whole circuit stops.

mcqs.q: In a parallel combination of resistances:
options: Current is the same and voltage is divided
Voltage is the same and current is divided
Both current and voltage are divided
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the voltage is the same across each resistance and the current is divided between them. That is why household appliances are joined in parallel: each gets the full voltage, and the others keep working when one is switched off. The equivalent resistance follows 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...

mcqs.q: If one resistance fails in a series circuit:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the whole circuit stops, because there is only one path for the current and it is broken. In a parallel circuit each appliance can be used separately, so a failure in one branch does not stop the others. This difference is a key point in the notes.

mcqs.q: Household appliances are joined in parallel so that:
options: Only one can run at a time
They share the voltage equally in series
Each gets the full voltage and works independently
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that each appliance gets the full voltage and the others keep working when one is switched off. In parallel the voltage is the same across every branch. This is the arrangement used in homes, as the notes explain.

mcqs.q: Resistances of 4 ohm, 6 ohm and 12 ohm in parallel across 6 V give an equivalent resistance of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2 ohm. From 1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12 = 6/12, so R = 2 ohm. The total current is then I = V / R = 6 / 2 = 3 A, as worked out in the notes.

mcqs.q: In the same parallel circuit (4, 6, 12 ohm across 6 V), the total current and branch currents are:
options: Total 3 A; branches 1.5 A, 1 A, 0.5 A
mcqs.why: The correct answer is total 3 A with branch currents 1.5 A, 1 A and 0.5 A. Each branch current is 6 divided by its own resistance: 6/4 = 1.5, 6/6 = 1, 6/12 = 0.5, and they add up to 3 A. This checks the rule that in parallel the current divides while the voltage stays the same.

mcqs.q: 6 ohm and 12 ohm joined in parallel give an equivalent resistance of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 4 ohm. From 1/R = 1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12, so R = 4 ohm. Note that a parallel combination always gives less than the smallest resistance in it, here less than 6 ohm.

mcqs.q: Joule's law gives the heat produced in a resistance as:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is H = I^2 R t. The energy wasted in a resistance comes out as heat; this is useful in a heater and a bulb, but a loss in wires. Electric power is related: P = V I = I^2 R = V^2 / R.

mcqs.q: Which set gives the correct formulas for electric power?
options: P = V I = I^2 R = V^2 / R
mcqs.why: The correct answer is P = V I = I^2 R = V^2 / R; all three forms are equivalent through Ohm's law. Any one of them can be used depending on which quantities are known. Power decides, for example, how bright a bulb is and how much current it draws.

mcqs.q: In a 220 V circuit, an 80 W bulb and a 120 W bulb are compared. Which has the greater resistance and which takes more current?
options: 80 W has greater resistance and more current
80 W has greater resistance; 120 W takes more current
120 W has greater resistance and more current
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the 80 W bulb has the greater resistance (605 ohm against 403 ohm from R = V^2 / P), and more current passes through the 120 W bulb (I = P / V). A lower wattage bulb at the same voltage is a higher resistance. This is the second worked example in the notes.

lessons.title: Household Electricity, Fuse and Safety
lessons.notes_html:
Three Wires of the Household Circuit

WireFunction
LiveThe wire that carries the voltage; touching it is dangerous
NeutralThe return path for the current; potential is about zero
EarthSafety wire; carries the fault current into the ground

Fuse

A fuse is a safety wire which melts and breaks the circuit when the current rises above a fixed limit. A fuse controls current, not voltage. It is always connected in series in the live wire.

Alternating Current (AC)

In AC the current reverses its direction at short intervals (50 times per second in Pakistan). Homes are supplied with AC because its voltage can easily be changed with a transformer.

Dangers of Electricity

  • Touching a wire with damaged insulation can give an electric shock
  • Connecting too many appliances to one socket overheats the wires and can cause a fire
  • Current passing through the human body affects the muscles and the heart, because the body is also a conductor

Safety Measures

  • Fit fuses and circuit breakers of the correct rating
  • Earth all metal appliances
  • Do not touch switches with wet hands; replace damaged wires at once
  • Avoid overloading and use good quality wires

mcqs.q: In the household circuit, the live wire is the one that:
options: Carries the voltage; touching it is dangerous
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the live wire carries the voltage, and touching it is dangerous. The neutral wire is the return path for the current with potential about zero. The earth wire is the safety wire that carries fault current into the ground.

mcqs.q: The neutral wire in a household circuit is:
options: The return path for the current, with potential about zero
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the return path for the current, with potential about zero. The live wire carries the voltage to the appliance, and the neutral completes the circuit back. The earth wire is separate and acts only as a safety path.

mcqs.q: The earth wire acts as a safety wire by:
options: Carrying the fault current into the ground
mcqs.why: The correct answer is carrying the fault current into the ground, so the user does not get a shock if a fault makes the metal body live. Metal appliances should therefore always be earthed. It works together with the fuse, not instead of it.

mcqs.q: A fuse is a safety wire that:
options: Melts and breaks the circuit when the current rises above a fixed limit
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it melts and breaks the circuit when the current rises above a fixed limit. A fuse controls current, not voltage. It is always connected in series in the live wire so that all the current passes through it.

mcqs.q: A fuse is always connected:
options: In parallel in the neutral wire
In series in the earth wire
In series in the live wire
mcqs.why: The correct answer is in series in the live wire. Being in series, the whole circuit current flows through the fuse, and being in the live wire, it disconnects the dangerous wire when it melts. A fuse of the correct rating should always be fitted.

mcqs.q: In AC, the current:
options: Reverses its direction at short intervals
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it reverses its direction at short intervals, 50 times per second in Pakistan. Homes are supplied with AC because its voltage can easily be changed with a transformer. DC, by contrast, flows steadily in one direction.

mcqs.q: Homes are supplied with AC rather than DC mainly because:
options: Its voltage can easily be changed with a transformer
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that AC voltage can easily be changed with a transformer, raised for transmission and lowered for home use. A transformer does not work on DC. This is the reason given in the notes for supplying homes with AC.

mcqs.q: Connecting too many appliances to one socket is dangerous because it:
options: Overheats the wires and can cause a fire
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it overheats the wires and can cause a fire; this is called overloading. Safety measures include avoiding overload and using good quality wires. Each socket and wire has a safe current limit that must not be exceeded.

mcqs.q: Current passing through the human body is dangerous because:
options: The body is also a conductor and current affects the muscles and the heart
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the body is also a conductor, and current through it affects the muscles and the heart. Touching a wire with damaged insulation can therefore give a serious electric shock. Damaged wires should be replaced at once for this reason.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a correct safety measure with electricity?
options: Earth all metal appliances and fit fuses of the correct rating
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to earth all metal appliances and fit fuses and circuit breakers of the correct rating. Switches must never be touched with wet hands, and damaged wires must be replaced at once. These measures are listed in the notes under dangers of electricity.

lessons.title: Magnetic Field and Force on a Current-Carrying Wire
lessons.notes_html:
Magnetic Field

  • Like poles repel each other; unlike poles attract each other
  • A single magnetic pole does not exist — even if a magnet is cut, each piece has both poles
  • Inside a bar magnet the field lines go from the south pole (S) to the north pole (N), and outside from N to S
  • The presence of a field is detected by the deflection of a compass needle

Force on a Current-Carrying Wire

When a current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field, a force acts on it. The force is maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the field.

F = B I L sin θ

  • Increasing the current I increases the force
  • The direction of the force is found by Fleming's left-hand rule

Worked Example

A 15 cm long wire carrying a current of 4 A is placed at an angle of 30° in a 0.8 T field. Find the force.

F = B I L sin θ = 0.8 × 4 × 0.15 × sin 30° = 0.8 × 4 × 0.15 × 0.5 = 0.24 N

Torque on a Coil

Equal and opposite forces act on the two sides of a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field, and they form a turning couple (torque) that rotates the coil. The D.C. motor and the galvanometer work on this same principle.

mcqs.q: A single magnetic pole:
options: Is found at the centre of a magnet
Does not exist; cutting a magnet gives each piece both poles
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that a single pole does not exist. Even if a magnet is cut into pieces, each piece has both a north and a south pole. Poles always occur in pairs, unlike electric charges which can be isolated.

mcqs.q: Inside a bar magnet, the field lines go from ______ and outside from ______.
options: N to S, S to N
N to N, S to S
Centre to ends, ends to centre
S to N, N to S
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: inside the magnet from south (S) to north (N), and outside from N to S. The lines thus form closed loops. The presence of a magnetic field is detected by the deflection of a compass needle.

mcqs.q: The presence of a magnetic field is detected by:
options: The deflection of a compass needle
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the deflection of a compass needle placed in the field. The needle turns to align with the field at that point. Like poles of magnets repel each other and unlike poles attract.

mcqs.q: When a current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field, the force on it is maximum when the wire is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is perpendicular to the field, as shown by F = B I L sin theta with sin 90 = 1. The force increases when the current I increases. Its direction is found by Fleming's left-hand rule.

mcqs.q: The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is F = B I L sin theta. Increasing the current I will:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is increase the force, because F is directly proportional to I. The force also depends on the field strength B, the length L of wire in the field, and the angle theta. Fleming's left-hand rule gives its direction.

mcqs.q: A 15 cm wire carrying 4 A at 30 degrees in a 0.8 T field experiences a force of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 0.24 N. From F = B I L sin theta = 0.8 x 4 x 0.15 x sin 30 = 0.8 x 4 x 0.15 x 0.5 = 0.24 N. This is the worked example in the notes for the force on a current-carrying wire.

mcqs.q: The direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is found by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Fleming's left-hand rule. It relates the directions of the magnetic field, the current and the resulting force (motion). This rule is used in explaining the working of the D.C. motor and the galvanometer.

mcqs.q: Equal and opposite forces on the two sides of a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field form:
options: A turning couple (torque) that rotates the coil
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a turning couple, or torque, that rotates the coil. The two sides of the coil carry current in opposite directions, so the forces on them are opposite and together they turn the coil. The D.C. motor and the galvanometer work on this same principle.

mcqs.q: The D.C. motor and the galvanometer both work on the principle of:
options: Torque on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the torque acting on a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field. The opposite forces on the two sides of the coil form a couple that rotates it. Induction, by contrast, is about generating an e.m.f. from a changing field.

mcqs.q: If the wire makes an angle of 30 degrees with the field instead of 90 degrees, the force is multiplied by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is sin 30 = 0.5, from the factor sin theta in F = B I L sin theta. That is why, in the worked example, the force came to half of its maximum value. The force is greatest at 90 degrees, where sin theta = 1.

lessons.title: D.C. Motor
lessons.notes_html:
What Does a D.C. Motor Do?

A D.C. motor converts electrical energy into mechanical (motion) energy. It works by the torque acting on a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field.

Parts of the Motor

PartFunction
ArmatureThe rotating coil wound on a soft iron core
CommutatorReverses the current in the coil after every half turn, so that rotation continues in the same direction
BrushesCarbon pieces that deliver current to the rotating commutator
MagnetProvides the permanent magnetic field

If there were no commutator, the torque would reverse after half a turn and the coil would only vibrate; it would not rotate.

mcqs.q: A D.C. motor converts:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is electrical energy into mechanical (motion) energy. It works by the torque acting on a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field. A generator does the opposite conversion, from mechanical to electrical energy.

mcqs.q: The rotating coil of a D.C. motor, wound on a soft iron core, is called the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the armature. It is the part that actually rotates when the torque acts on the coil. The soft iron core strengthens the effect of the coil's field.

mcqs.q: The function of the commutator in a D.C. motor is to:
options: Stop the current after each turn
Reverse the current in the coil after every half turn so rotation continues in the same direction
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to reverse the current in the coil after every half turn, so that the torque keeps acting in the same sense and rotation continues in the same direction. Without it, the motor would not keep rotating. The brushes deliver current to this rotating commutator.

mcqs.q: The brushes in a D.C. motor are:
options: Carbon pieces that deliver current to the rotating commutator
Iron rods fixed to the coil
mcqs.why: The correct answer is carbon pieces that deliver current to the rotating commutator while it spins. They stay in contact with the commutator as it turns. The magnet in the motor provides the permanent magnetic field in which the coil rotates.

mcqs.q: If a D.C. motor had no commutator, the coil would:
options: Only vibrate, because the torque would reverse after half a turn
Rotate in the opposite direction steadily
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it would only vibrate; the torque would reverse after every half turn, so the coil could not keep rotating. The commutator prevents this by reversing the current at exactly that moment. This is stated directly in the notes on the D.C. motor.

mcqs.q: In a D.C. motor, the permanent magnetic field is provided by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the magnet. The coil rotates inside the field of this magnet, and the force on its current-carrying sides produces the torque. The armature, commutator and brushes each have their own separate jobs in the motor.

mcqs.q: The motor works on the same principle as the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the galvanometer: both work on the torque acting on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field. In the galvanometer the coil's deflection measures current, while in the motor the continuous torque produces rotation. The commutator is what turns the galvanometer principle into a motor.

mcqs.q: After every half turn of the coil in a D.C. motor, the commutator:
options: Reverses the current in the coil
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it reverses the current in the coil. Because the current reverses just as the coil passes the vertical position, the forces on its sides keep turning it the same way. Rotation therefore continues in the same direction turn after turn.

mcqs.q: The part of the D.C. motor that rotates is the:
options: Armature (coil on a soft iron core)
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the armature, the coil wound on a soft iron core. The brushes are stationary carbon pieces, and the magnet is fixed. Only the armature, together with the commutator attached to its axle, rotates.

mcqs.q: A D.C. motor is run from a direct current supply. Its rotation is continuous mainly because of the:
options: Commutator reversing the current each half turn
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the commutator reversing the current each half turn. The core, brushes and magnet are all necessary, but without the commutator's reversal the torque would reverse and the coil would only vibrate. The commutator is therefore the key to continuous rotation.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Induction
lessons.notes_html:
What is Induction?

When the magnetic field linked with a circuit changes, an electric force (induced e.m.f.) and current are produced in the circuit. This is called electromagnetic induction (Faraday's law).

Experiment

Join a coil to a galvanometer and move a magnet in and out of the coil: the needle deflects, i.e. a current is produced. If the magnet is stationary, the current is zero. For maximum voltage the wire should be moved perpendicular to the field (cutting the field).

Ways to Increase the Induced e.m.f.

  • Move the magnet faster
  • Use a stronger magnet
  • Increase the turns of the coil
  • Use a soft iron core

Lenz's Law

The direction of the induced current is such that it opposes the change that produces it. This agrees with the law of conservation of energy: the mechanical work done in pushing the magnet becomes electrical energy.

Mutual Induction

A changing current in one coil produces an e.m.f. in a nearby second coil. Example: a transformer works on this same principle.

Worked Example

One coil is wound around another coil (solenoid). The current in the first changes at the rate of 150 A/s and the mutual inductance is 5.5 × 10^-5 H. Find the e.m.f. induced in the second coil.

e = M × (ΔI / Δt) = 5.5 × 10^-5 × 150 = 8.25 × 10^-3 V

mcqs.q: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an induced e.m.f. and current in a circuit when:
options: The magnetic field linked with the circuit changes
mcqs.why: The correct answer is when the magnetic field linked with the circuit changes; this is Faraday's law. Moving a magnet in and out of a coil joined to a galvanometer makes the needle deflect, showing a current is produced. If the magnet is stationary, the current is zero.

mcqs.q: In the coil-and-magnet experiment, if the magnet is held stationary inside the coil, the induced current is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is zero, because the field linked with the coil is not changing. Induction needs change: the needle of the galvanometer deflects only while the magnet moves in or out. This is the central observation behind Faraday's law.

mcqs.q: Which of these increases the induced e.m.f.?
options: Using fewer turns of the coil
mcqs.why: The correct answer is moving the magnet faster. The induced e.m.f. also increases with a stronger magnet, more turns of the coil, and a soft iron core. All of these make the field linked with the circuit change more strongly.

mcqs.q: For maximum induced voltage, the wire should be moved:
options: In a circle around the magnet
Perpendicular to the field, cutting the field
mcqs.why: The correct answer is perpendicular to the field, so that it cuts the field lines. Cutting more field lines per second means a greater change of the linked field. Moving parallel to the field cuts no lines and gives no e.m.f.

mcqs.q: Lenz's law states that the direction of the induced current is such that it:
options: Opposes the change that produces it
Is always equal to the magnet's motion
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it opposes the change that produces it. This agrees with the law of conservation of energy: the mechanical work done in pushing the magnet becomes the electrical energy produced. If the induced current helped the change, energy would be created from nothing.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, Lenz's law agrees with the law of conservation of energy because:
options: No work is needed to move the magnet
The mechanical work done in pushing the magnet becomes electrical energy
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the mechanical work done in pushing the magnet against the opposing induced effects becomes the electrical energy. The opposition described by Lenz's law is exactly what makes us do that work. So energy is converted, not created.

mcqs.q: Mutual induction is when:
options: A changing current in one coil produces an e.m.f. in a nearby second coil
A magnet induces current in its own coil only
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that a changing current in one coil produces an e.m.f. in a nearby second coil. A transformer works on this same principle. The two coils are not joined by any wire; the changing field links them.

mcqs.q: The transformer works on the principle of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is mutual induction: the changing current in the primary coil induces an e.m.f. in the secondary coil. This is why a transformer needs AC, whose current changes continuously. On steady DC there would be no continuous induction.

mcqs.q: The current in the first coil changes at 150 A/s and the mutual inductance is 5.5 x 10^-5 H. The e.m.f. induced in the second coil is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 8.25 x 10^-3 V. From e = M x (change of I / change of t) = 5.5 x 10^-5 x 150 = 8.25 x 10^-3 V. This is the worked example of mutual induction given in the notes.

mcqs.q: To increase the induced e.m.f. in a coil, one should:
options: Increase the turns of the coil
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to increase the turns of the coil; more turns mean more of the changing field is linked, so the e.m.f. is larger. A stronger magnet, faster motion and a soft iron core also help, as listed in the notes.

lessons.title: A.C. Generator and Transformer
lessons.notes_html:
A.C. Generator

A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. When a coil rotates in a magnetic field, the field linked with it changes continuously and alternating current (AC) is produced by electromagnetic induction. The ends of the coil are connected to the external circuit through slip rings and brushes.

Transformer

A transformer increases or decreases AC voltage on the principle of mutual induction. It does not work on DC, because the field does not change in DC.

Vs / Vp = Ns / Np

Step-upStep-down
Ns > Np; voltage increasesNs < Np; voltage decreases
For transmission from the power stationBefore supplying to homes

Worked Example

A transformer has to change 220 V to 12 V. The primary coil has 2200 turns. Find the turns of the secondary.

Ns = Np × Vs / Vp = 2200 × 12 / 220 = 120 turns

Role of the Transformer in Power Transmission

  • At the power station a step-up transformer raises the voltage, so the current decreases and energy loss in the wires (I^2R) becomes small
  • At the city and neighbourhood a step-down transformer reduces the voltage to 220 V and supplies it to homes
  • Small step-down transformers are also present inside chargers etc. in the home

mcqs.q: An A.C. generator converts:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is mechanical energy into electrical energy. When a coil rotates in a magnetic field, the field linked with it changes continuously and alternating current is produced by electromagnetic induction. A motor does the reverse conversion.

mcqs.q: In an A.C. generator, the ends of the coil are connected to the external circuit through:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is slip rings and brushes. The slip rings rotate with the coil and keep the same end of the coil connected to the same side of the circuit, so the output alternates. A D.C. machine uses a commutator instead, which reverses the connections.

mcqs.q: A transformer is used to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to increase or decrease AC voltage, on the principle of mutual induction. It does not work on DC, because the field does not change in DC. Its voltages and turns follow Vs / Vp = Ns / Np.

mcqs.q: A transformer does not work on DC because:
options: The magnetic field does not change in DC
DC cannot pass through a coil
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the magnetic field does not change in DC, so no e.m.f. is induced in the secondary coil by mutual induction. With AC the field changes continuously, which is exactly what induction requires. This is the reason stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: In a step-up transformer:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Ns > Np and the voltage increases, from Vs / Vp = Ns / Np. Step-up transformers are used for transmission from the power station. A step-down transformer has Ns < Np and decreases the voltage, as used before supplying homes.

mcqs.q: A transformer must change 220 V to 12 V, and its primary has 2200 turns. The secondary turns are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 120 turns. From Ns = Np x Vs / Vp = 2200 x 12 / 220 = 120 turns. This is the worked example in the notes, and since the voltage is stepped down, the secondary naturally has far fewer turns than the primary.

mcqs.q: At the power station, a step-up transformer raises the voltage so that:
options: The current decreases and energy loss in the wires (I^2 R) becomes small
The current increases and losses grow
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the current decreases and the energy loss in the wires, which goes as I^2 R, becomes small. Transmitting at high voltage and low current wastes far less energy as heat. Near homes, step-down transformers then reduce the voltage to 220 V.

mcqs.q: Before electricity is supplied to homes, the voltage is reduced to 220 V by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a step-down transformer at the city and neighbourhood level. Small step-down transformers are also present inside chargers and similar devices in the home. The transmission system therefore uses both kinds of transformer at different stages.

mcqs.q: The turns ratio of a transformer is given by:
options: Vs x Vp = Ns x Np
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Vs / Vp = Ns / Np: the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio. This one relation solves transformer problems, such as finding 120 secondary turns for 2200 primary turns when stepping 220 V down to 12 V. It rests on the principle of mutual induction.

mcqs.q: The alternating current in a generator is produced because:
options: The rotating coil's linked field changes continuously
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that as the coil rotates in the magnetic field, the field linked with it changes continuously, so an alternating e.m.f. is induced. The slip rings merely carry this current to the external circuit unchanged in character. The induction itself follows Faraday's law.

lessons.title: Digital and Analogue Electronics
lessons.notes_html:
What is Electronics?

Electronics is a combined field of physics, engineering and technology in which work is taken by controlling the flow of electrons.

Analogue and Digital Signals

AnalogueDigital
Continuously changing quantity; countless valuesOnly two states: 0 and 1
Examples: temperature of a thermometer, hands of a clockExamples: computer, mobile, digital clock

A digital signal is in only one of two states (0 or 1), so it is safer from the effect of noise and more accurate.

Advantages of Digital Devices

  • Greater accuracy and reliability
  • Data is easy to store and send
  • Small size and low power consumption

The world is moving from low-technology devices to high-technology devices: for example, from writing letters to e-mail, and from film cameras to digital cameras.

Vacuum Tube and DAC

  • Vacuum Tube — an early device of electronics; the first radios and computers were made with them
  • DAC (Digital to Analogue Converter) — converts a digital signal into analogue, for example to give sound to a speaker

mcqs.q: Electronics is a field in which work is taken by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is controlling the flow of electrons. Electronics is a combined field of physics, engineering and technology built on this idea. All electronic devices, from radios to computers, work by guiding electron flow.

mcqs.q: An analogue signal is a:
options: Quantity with only two states, 0 and 1
Continuously changing quantity with countless values
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a continuously changing quantity with countless values, such as the temperature of a thermometer or the hands of a clock. A digital signal is the restricted one, having only two states. The two kinds of signal are contrasted in the notes.

mcqs.q: A digital signal can be in only one of two states:
options: High and low voltage only in AC
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 0 and 1. Because it has only two states, a digital signal is safer from the effect of noise and more accurate than an analogue signal. Computers, mobile phones and digital clocks all work with digital signals.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a digital device or signal user?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the computer and mobile phone, which use digital signals with two states 0 and 1. The hands of a clock and a thermometer give continuously changing analogue values instead. This contrast is used in the notes to separate analogue from digital.

mcqs.q: One advantage of digital devices is:
options: Large size and high power use
mcqs.why: The correct answer is greater accuracy and reliability. Digital data is also easy to store and send, and digital devices are small in size with low power consumption. These advantages are why the world is moving from low-technology to high-technology devices.

mcqs.q: A DAC (Digital to Analogue Converter) is used to:
options: Convert a digital signal into analogue, e.g. to give sound to a speaker
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to convert a digital signal into an analogue one, for example to give sound to a speaker. A speaker needs a continuously varying (analogue) signal, while the stored music is digital. The DAC bridges these two forms.

mcqs.q: The earliest electronic devices, such as the first radios and computers, were made with:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is vacuum tubes, an early device of electronics. The first radios and computers were built with them before modern components took over. Thermionic emission inside such tubes is studied in the next lesson.

mcqs.q: Digital signals are safer from the effect of noise because:
options: They have only two states, 0 and 1, which are easy to recognise
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that with only two states, 0 and 1, the receiving device can still recognise which state was sent even if noise is added. An analogue signal, with countless values, is distorted by any small noise. This is a key advantage of digital systems in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which pair gives only analogue examples?
options: Temperature of a thermometer, hands of a clock
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the temperature of a thermometer and the hands of a clock; both change continuously and can take countless values. Computers, mobiles and digital clocks are the digital examples given in the notes. Analogue and digital are the two basic kinds of signal.

mcqs.q: Data in digital devices is:
options: Always lost when power goes off
mcqs.why: The correct answer is easy to store and send, which is one of the listed advantages of digital devices. Together with greater accuracy and reliability and small size with low power consumption, this explains the shift to digital technology. Examples in the notes include moving from letters to e-mail and from film cameras to digital cameras.

lessons.title: Thermionic Emission and Cathode Rays
lessons.notes_html:
Thermionic Emission

The emission of electrons from the surface of a hot metal is called thermionic emission. In a vacuum tube the filament heats the cathode, and the cathode emits electrons.

  • A vacuum is essential for emission; if there were air, the electrons would collide with air molecules and the cathode would oxidise
  • In a metal the charge carriers are free electrons (not protons or neutrons)

Cathode Rays

The stream of electrons emitted from the cathode is called cathode rays.

Properties of Cathode Rays

  • They are negatively charged electrons
  • They travel in straight lines and form shadows
  • They are deflected in electric and magnetic fields
  • Their properties do not change if the type of gas or the material of the cathode is changed — the same electrons come out of every material
  • The electron was discovered from the study of cathode rays

Attraction Towards the Anode

When the anode is given a positive voltage compared with the cathode, the electrons are attracted towards it and accelerated, because opposite charges attract.

mcqs.q: Thermionic emission is the emission of electrons from:
options: The surface of a hot metal
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the surface of a hot metal. In a vacuum tube, the filament heats the cathode and the cathode emits electrons. Heating gives the electrons enough energy to leave the metal surface.

mcqs.q: In a vacuum tube, the electrons are emitted by the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the cathode, after the filament heats it. A vacuum is essential for this emission. The emitted electrons then travel through the tube as cathode rays.

mcqs.q: A vacuum is essential in a vacuum tube because, if there were air:
options: Electrons would collide with air molecules and the cathode would oxidise
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the electrons would collide with air molecules and the cathode would oxidise. Both effects would spoil the emission. This is why the tube is emptied of air before it is sealed.

mcqs.q: In a metal, the charge carriers are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is free electrons, not protons or neutrons. These free electrons move through the metal and carry the current, and they are also what thermionic emission releases from a hot surface. Protons and neutrons stay in the nuclei of the metal atoms.

mcqs.q: Cathode rays are a stream of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is electrons emitted from the cathode. They are negatively charged and travel in straight lines. The electron itself was discovered from the study of cathode rays.

mcqs.q: Which is a property of cathode rays?
options: They depend on the gas used
They travel in straight lines and form shadows
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they travel in straight lines and form shadows, like light. They are negatively charged electrons and are deflected in electric and magnetic fields. Their properties do not change with the type of gas or the cathode material.

mcqs.q: Cathode rays are deflected by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is electric and magnetic fields, because the rays are moving charged particles (electrons). This deflection is used to steer the beam in the cathode ray oscilloscope. A neutral ray, such as gamma radiation, would not be deflected in this way.

mcqs.q: The properties of cathode rays do not change when the gas or cathode material is changed. This shows that:
options: The same electrons come out of every material
Cathode rays are waves of the gas
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the same electrons come out of every material. This universality helped establish that electrons are a basic part of all matter. It was from the study of cathode rays that the electron was discovered.

mcqs.q: When the anode is given a positive voltage compared with the cathode, the electrons:
options: Are attracted towards the anode and accelerated
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they are attracted towards the anode and accelerated, because opposite charges attract. The positive anode pulls the negative electrons across the tube. This is how the electron beam gains its speed in tubes and in the electron gun.

mcqs.q: The electron was discovered from the study of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is cathode rays. Experiments on these rays showed they are negatively charged particles found in every material, the electrons. Their deflection in electric and magnetic fields revealed their charge and behaviour.

lessons.title: Electron Gun and Cathode Ray Oscilloscope
lessons.notes_html:
Electron Gun

An electron gun produces a narrow and fast beam of electrons. Its parts:

  • Filament — heats the cathode
  • Cathode — emits electrons (thermionic emission)
  • Anode — accelerates the electrons with its positive voltage and the beam moves forward
  • Grid and focusing system — makes the beam narrow and focuses it on the target

Deflection of the Beam in an Electric Field

When the electron beam passes between two plates it bends towards the positive plate. Reversing the direction of the field also reverses the direction of bending. By this principle the beam is moved up and down (Y plates) in the CRO.

Beam in a Magnetic Field

  • A magnetic field bends the beam (a force acts on it)
  • But the speed and energy of the beam do not change, because the force always acts perpendicular to the motion and does no work

The presence of an electric field can be detected by the deflection of a charged particle (for example an electron).

Cathode Ray Oscilloscope (CRO)

PartFunction
Fluorescent screenMakes a glowing spot where the beam strikes; the shape of the signal is seen
CathodeEmits electrons
AnodeAccelerates the electrons and forms the beam
Y platesBend the beam vertically (up and down); the signal is applied to them

The CRO is an instrument for seeing and measuring the shape of electrical signals. The picture in old TVs and monitors was also formed by cathode rays.

mcqs.q: An electron gun produces:
options: A narrow and fast beam of electrons
Cathode rays in all directions only
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a narrow and fast beam of electrons. Its parts work together: the filament heats the cathode, the cathode emits electrons, the anode accelerates them, and the grid and focusing system make the beam narrow. Such a gun is the heart of the CRO.

mcqs.q: In the electron gun, the filament's job is to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to heat the cathode, so that the cathode emits electrons by thermionic emission. The anode then accelerates the electrons with its positive voltage. Heating is therefore the first step in producing the beam.

mcqs.q: The anode in an electron gun:
options: Accelerates the electrons with its positive voltage
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it accelerates the electrons with its positive voltage, so the beam moves forward fast. Being positive, the anode attracts the negative electrons. The cathode, not the anode, is the part that emits the electrons.

mcqs.q: The grid and focusing system of the electron gun serve to:
options: Make the beam narrow and focus it on the target
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to make the beam narrow and focus it on the target. Without focusing, the electrons would spread out and no sharp spot could be formed. A sharp spot is essential for the clear trace seen on a CRO screen.

mcqs.q: When the electron beam passes between two charged plates, it bends:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is towards the positive plate, because electrons are negatively charged and opposite charges attract. Reversing the direction of the field also reverses the direction of bending. By this principle the beam is moved up and down by the Y plates in the CRO.

mcqs.q: A magnetic field bends the electron beam, but the speed and energy of the beam do not change because:
options: The magnetic force is very weak
The force always acts perpendicular to the motion and does no work
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the magnetic force always acts perpendicular to the motion and so does no work on the electrons. It changes their direction only, not their speed. An electric field, in contrast, can accelerate the beam and change its energy.

mcqs.q: In a CRO, the fluorescent screen:
options: Makes a glowing spot where the beam strikes, showing the shape of the signal
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it makes a glowing spot where the beam strikes, and the shape of the signal is seen from the spot's movement. The CRO is an instrument for seeing and measuring the shape of electrical signals. Old TVs and monitors also formed their picture by cathode rays.

mcqs.q: The Y plates in a CRO are used to:
options: Bend the beam vertically (up and down); the signal is applied to them
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to bend the beam vertically, up and down, and the signal under study is applied to them. As the signal voltage changes, the spot moves up and down accordingly. Combined with the horizontal sweep, this draws the waveform on the screen.

mcqs.q: The cathode ray oscilloscope (CRO) is an instrument for:
options: Seeing and measuring the shape of electrical signals
mcqs.why: The correct answer is seeing and measuring the shape of electrical signals. Its electron gun, deflection plates and fluorescent screen work together to draw the signal. The presence of an electric field can likewise be detected by the deflection of a charged particle such as an electron.

mcqs.q: Reversing the direction of the electric field between the deflection plates:
options: Has no effect on the beam
Reverses the direction of bending of the beam
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it reverses the direction of bending, because the beam always bends towards whichever plate is positive. This controlled bending moves the spot up and down in the CRO. It is the basis of how the Y plates display a changing signal.

lessons.title: Logic Gates
lessons.notes_html:
What is Logic?

Logic is the system of thinking in which a decision is made on two states — true/false, yes/no, 1/0. Example: “If it rains and I have an umbrella, I will go to school” — such decisions are taken with gates in digital circuits.

Logic Gate

A logic gate is the basic component of digital electronics which performs a logic operation on one or more inputs and gives one output.

Main Gates and Truth Tables

GateBoolean ExpressionRule
ANDX = A . BOutput is 1 when both inputs are 1
ORX = A + BOutput is 1 when any one input is 1
NOT (Inverter)X = ĀOutput is the opposite of the input
NANDX = opposite of (A . B)The opposite of AND
NORX = opposite of (A + B)The opposite of OR
ABANDORNANDNOR
000011
010110
100110
111100

The NOT gate is a gate with only one input which uses the inverted input: if the input is 1 the output is 0, and if the input is 0 the output is 1.

The gates that give output 0 for inputs 1 and 0 are AND and NOR.

mcqs.q: A logic gate is a basic component of digital electronics that:
options: Performs a logic operation on one or more inputs and gives one output
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it performs a logic operation on one or more inputs and gives one output. Logic is the system of decisions on two states: true/false, yes/no, 1/0. Gates are the building blocks with which digital circuits make such decisions.

mcqs.q: For an AND gate (X = A . B), the output is 1 when:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is when both inputs are 1. If either input is 0, the AND output is 0. This matches the example type of decision: both conditions must be true together for the result to be true.

mcqs.q: For an OR gate (X = A + B), the output is 1 when:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is when any one input is 1; the output is 0 only if both inputs are 0. The OR gate is therefore less strict than the AND gate. Its truth table rows are 0,0 -> 0 and all other rows -> 1.

mcqs.q: A NOT gate (inverter) has:
options: Only one input, and its output is the opposite of the input
mcqs.why: The correct answer is only one input, with the output the opposite of the input: input 1 gives output 0, and input 0 gives output 1. Its Boolean expression is X = A with a bar over A. It is the simplest of all the gates.

mcqs.q: A NAND gate gives the opposite of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is AND: NAND is the opposite of (A . B). So for inputs 1 and 1, where AND gives 1, NAND gives 0. For all other input pairs NAND gives 1, as the truth table in the notes shows.

mcqs.q: A NOR gate gives the opposite of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is OR: NOR is the opposite of (A + B). So NOR gives 1 only when both inputs are 0, and 0 for every other combination. The gates that give output 0 for inputs 1 and 0 are AND and NOR, as noted in the lesson.

mcqs.q: For inputs A = 1, B = 1, the outputs of AND, OR, NAND and NOR are respectively:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is AND 1, OR 1, NAND 0, NOR 0, exactly as in the last row of the truth table in the notes. NAND and NOR are simply the opposites of AND and OR. With both inputs 1, both basic gates are satisfied, so their opposites give 0.

mcqs.q: For inputs A = 0, B = 0, the NAND and NOR outputs are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 1 and 1, from the first row of the truth table. AND and OR both give 0 for 0,0 inputs, so their opposites, NAND and NOR, both give 1. This row shows clearly how the inverted gates behave oppositely to the basic gates.

mcqs.q: For inputs A = 1, B = 0, which gates give output 0?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is AND and NOR, as the notes point out. AND gives 0 because one input is 0, and NOR gives 0 because one input is 1 (so OR is 1 and its opposite is 0). OR and NAND both give 1 for this input pair.

mcqs.q: The Boolean expression for an OR gate is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is X = A + B, where the + sign stands for the OR operation, not ordinary addition. AND is written X = A . B, and NOT is written with a bar over the input. These expressions are listed with the main gates in the notes.

lessons.title: Data, Information and ICT
lessons.notes_html:
Data and Information

DataInformation
Raw figures, letters and facts with no arrangementData that has been arranged and processed and gives meaning and benefit
Example: 85, "Ahmed", 12Example: "Ahmed got 85 marks in the examination"

Information Cycle

Input, processing, output and storage of a computer together are called the information cycle:

  • Input — giving data with keyboard, mouse, etc.
  • Processing — working on the data in the CPU
  • Output — the result on screen, printer, etc.
  • Storage — keeping the data safe

What is ICT?

ICT stands for Information and Communication Technology. It is the technology with which information is collected, stored, sent from one place to another and used — computers, mobile phones, the internet, radio and TV all come in it.

Parts of IT

  • Hardware — physical parts
  • Software — programs
  • Data / Information — that on which work is done
  • Communication network — the means of transferring data

mcqs.q: Data is best described as:
options: Raw figures, letters and facts with no arrangement
mcqs.why: The correct answer is raw figures, letters and facts with no arrangement, such as 85, 'Ahmed', 12 by themselves. When data is arranged and processed so that it gives meaning and benefit, it becomes information. For example, 'Ahmed got 85 marks in the examination' is information.

mcqs.q: Information is:
options: Data that has been arranged and processed and gives meaning and benefit
mcqs.why: The correct answer is data that has been arranged and processed and gives meaning and benefit. The raw items 85, 'Ahmed' and 12 become information when combined into 'Ahmed got 85 marks in the examination'. Processing is what turns data into information.

mcqs.q: The information cycle of a computer consists of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is input, processing, output and storage, taken together. Data is given in by keyboard or mouse, worked on in the CPU, shown as a result on screen or printer, and kept safe in storage. All four stages together form the information cycle.

mcqs.q: In the information cycle, processing is done in the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the CPU, where the data is worked on according to the program. Input devices such as the keyboard and mouse only give the data, and the output appears on the screen or printer. Storage keeps the data safe for later use.

mcqs.q: ICT stands for:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Information and Communication Technology. It is the technology with which information is collected, stored, sent from one place to another and used. Computers, mobile phones, the internet, radio and TV all come under ICT.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a part of IT in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the furniture of the office. The parts of IT are hardware (physical parts), software (programs), data/information (that on which work is done) and the communication network (the means of transferring data). These four together make the system work.

mcqs.q: In ICT, the communication network is:
options: The physical parts of the computer
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the means of transferring data from one place to another. Hardware is the physical parts and software is the programs; the network is what carries data between them. Without a network, computers would work only in isolation.

mcqs.q: Which group all comes under ICT as given in the notes?
options: Computers, mobile phones, the internet, radio and TV
mcqs.why: The correct answer is computers, mobile phones, the internet, radio and TV. ICT covers every technology used to collect, store, send and use information. It is therefore much wider than computers alone.

mcqs.q: 'Ahmed got 85 marks in the examination' is an example of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is information, because the raw data items 85, 'Ahmed' and 12 have been arranged and processed into a meaningful statement. By itself, 85 is only data. The meaning and benefit are what make the difference.

mcqs.q: Output in the information cycle means:
options: The result shown on screen, printer, etc.
Working on data in the CPU
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the result shown on the screen, printer and similar devices. Input is giving data with keyboard or mouse, processing is working on it in the CPU, and storage is keeping it safe. Each stage of the cycle has its own distinct role.

lessons.title: Computer — Hardware, Software and Memory
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Computer?

A computer is an electronic device which takes data, works on it quickly and correctly according to given instructions (programs), gives the result and stores it. In daily life it has a big role in education, banking, hospitals, ticketing and communication.

Hardware and Software

HardwareSoftware
Physical parts that can be touched: CPU, monitor, keyboardPrograms and instructions: Windows, MS Word
  • System software — operating system, compiler, interpreter, assembler
  • Application software — MS Word, Tally, etc.
  • A compiler translates the whole program into machine language at once; an interpreter does the same work line by line and at the same time
  • A sequence of instructions given a name to get the desired result is a program; the step-by-step plan of instructions is called an algorithm

Types of Memory

Primary MemorySecondary Memory
RAM and ROM — directly connected to the CPU, fastHard disk, USB, CD — large capacity, permanent storage
RAMROM
Temporary; data is lost when the power goes offPermanent; data stays safe even when the power goes off
Holds running programs and dataStart-up instructions (BIOS)

Storage devices: hard disk (large capacity, reliable), floppy disk (small capacity, less reliable), USB flash drive, CD/DVD. The hard disk is more reliable than the floppy disk.

Types of Computer and Other Terms

  • Supercomputer — the most powerful; another name for a large computer is mainframe
  • USB = Universal Serial Bus
  • MS Word file extensions: .doc, .docx, .rtf — .jpeg is an image extension

mcqs.q: A computer is an electronic device which:
options: Takes data, works on it quickly and correctly according to programs, gives the result and stores it
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it takes data, works on it quickly and correctly according to given instructions (programs), gives the result and stores it. It has a big role in daily life: education, banking, hospitals, ticketing and communication. Programs are essential to its working.

mcqs.q: Hardware means:
options: Physical parts that can be touched, such as CPU, monitor and keyboard
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the physical parts that can be touched, like the CPU, monitor and keyboard. Software is the opposite: programs and instructions such as Windows and MS Word, which cannot be touched. Both are needed for a computer to work.

mcqs.q: Which of these is system software?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the operating system and the language tools: compiler, interpreter and assembler. Application software, by contrast, includes programs like MS Word and Tally that do specific jobs for the user. System software manages the computer itself.

mcqs.q: A compiler differs from an interpreter because a compiler:
options: Translates the whole program into machine language at once
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that a compiler translates the whole program into machine language at once, while an interpreter does the same work line by line and at the same time. Both are system software. The choice affects how a program is checked and run.

mcqs.q: A sequence of instructions given a name to get the desired result is a ______; the step-by-step plan of instructions is an ______.
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the sequence of instructions is a program, and the step-by-step plan is called an algorithm. The algorithm is the plan worked out first, and the program is that plan written for the computer. Both definitions are given in the notes on software.

mcqs.q: RAM is a primary memory in which:
options: Data stays safe when power goes off
Data is temporary and is lost when the power goes off
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that data in RAM is temporary and is lost when the power goes off; RAM holds the running programs and data. ROM is the permanent primary memory whose data stays safe and which holds start-up instructions (BIOS). Primary memory is directly connected to the CPU and is fast.

mcqs.q: ROM holds:
options: Start-up instructions (BIOS), and its data stays even when power goes off
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the start-up instructions (BIOS), and the data in ROM stays safe even when the power goes off. RAM holds the running programs and data but loses them without power. Both RAM and ROM are primary memory, directly connected to the CPU.

mcqs.q: Hard disk, USB and CD are examples of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is secondary memory, which has large capacity and permanent storage. The hard disk has large capacity and is reliable, while the floppy disk has small capacity and is less reliable. Secondary memory keeps data safe when the computer is off.

mcqs.q: A supercomputer is:
options: The most powerful computer; a large computer is also called a mainframe
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the most powerful computer, and another name for a large computer is a mainframe. USB stands for Universal Serial Bus. These terms are listed in the notes on types of computer.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT an MS Word file extension according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is .jpeg, which is an image extension, not a Word document extension. MS Word files use .doc, .docx and .rtf. Recognising extensions helps tell document files apart from picture files.

lessons.title: Means of Communication, Networks and the Internet
lessons.notes_html:
Transmission of Radio Waves

A transmitter sends radio waves into space; they reach the radio receiver travelling along the surface of the Earth, reflected from the ionosphere as sky waves, or in a straight line. For this reason radio broadcasts are heard over long distances.

Light Signals in Optical Fibre

In an optical fibre, light signals travel forward by total internal reflection: the light keeps reflecting inside the dense inner part of the fibre and reaches the end. Advantages:

  • Very high speed and large capacity
  • Very little loss of signal
  • Safe from electrical noise and interference

For this reason optical fibre is more useful for communication than traditional copper wires.

Computer Network

LANMANWAN
Inside one building / officeInside one cityUp to countries and continents

LAN is best for connecting computers inside office buildings.

Internet

The internet is the interconnected network of computers all over the world. Through it, information, education, contact, shopping and government services are available sitting at home. The role of IT in school education: digital lessons, online books, results and teacher–student contact.

mcqs.q: Radio broadcasts are heard over long distances partly because the waves can travel:
options: Along the Earth's surface, reflected from the ionosphere as sky waves, or in a straight line
Only in a straight line to the receiver
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that a transmitter sends radio waves into space, and they reach the receiver along the surface of the Earth, reflected from the ionosphere as sky waves, or in a straight line. These paths explain long-distance radio reception. Optical fibres carry light signals, not radio broadcasts.

mcqs.q: In an optical fibre, light signals travel forward by:
options: Total internal reflection inside the dense inner part of the fibre
mcqs.why: The correct answer is total internal reflection: the light keeps reflecting inside the dense inner part of the fibre and reaches the end. This gives very high speed and large capacity with very little loss of signal. It is the same principle studied in the optics chapter.

mcqs.q: An advantage of optical fibre over traditional copper wires is:
options: Very little loss of signal and safety from electrical noise
mcqs.why: The correct answer is very little loss of signal, together with very high speed, large capacity, and safety from electrical noise and interference. For these reasons optical fibre is more useful for communication than traditional copper wires. The notes list exactly these advantages.

mcqs.q: A LAN is a network spread over:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is inside one building or office. A MAN covers one city and a WAN extends up to countries and continents. LAN is therefore best for connecting computers inside office buildings, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: A WAN extends:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is up to countries and continents; it is the widest type of network. A LAN covers one building or office and a MAN covers one city. The internet itself is the interconnected network of computers all over the world.

mcqs.q: The internet is:
options: The interconnected network of computers all over the world
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the interconnected network of computers all over the world. Through it, information, education, contact, shopping and government services are available sitting at home. It is far bigger than any LAN, MAN or single WAN in scope.

mcqs.q: A MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) covers:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is one city. LAN, MAN and WAN are arranged by size: building, city, then countries and continents. Remembering this order makes it easy to classify any network described in a question.

mcqs.q: For connecting computers inside office buildings, the best network type is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is LAN, the local area network, which is designed for one building or office. A WAN would be unnecessarily large and costly for this purpose. This application is stated directly in the notes.

mcqs.q: The role of IT in school education, as given in the notes, includes:
options: Digital lessons, online books, results and teacher-student contact
mcqs.why: The correct answer is digital lessons, online books, results and teacher-student contact. IT supports schooling in these practical ways. It is presented in the notes as a help to education, not as a replacement for schools.

mcqs.q: Optical fibre communication is safer than copper wire from:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is electrical noise and interference, because the signal in a fibre is light, not electric current. Combined with very high speed, large capacity and very little loss, this makes fibre more useful for communication. Copper wires pick up electrical interference easily by comparison.

lessons.title: Structure of the Atom and Rutherford's Model
lessons.notes_html:
Fundamental Particles of the Atom

ParticleChargeMass / Place
Proton+1In the nucleus; mass about 1 u
Neutron0 (no charge)In the nucleus; mass about equal to the proton
Electron−1Around the nucleus; mass very small
  • The proton and the electron have charges equal in magnitude and opposite in sign
  • The proton and the neutron have nearly equal masses
  • Almost the whole mass of the atom is in the nucleus; the nucleus is very small in size but heavy in mass
  • In a neutral atom, protons and electrons are equal

Geiger–Marsden Experiment and Rutherford Model

Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at a gold foil: most particles passed straight through, some were deflected and very few bounced back. From this Rutherford concluded:

  • Most of the atom is empty (most particles passed straight through)
  • The whole positive charge and mass are gathered in a small nucleus in the centre
  • Electrons revolve around the nucleus

Any element is identified by its number of protons; if the protons change, the element itself changes.

mcqs.q: The charge and location of a proton are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is charge +1 and located in the nucleus, with a mass of about 1 u. The neutron is also in the nucleus but has no charge. The electron, with charge -1, moves around the nucleus.

mcqs.q: The neutron has:
options: No charge, and mass about equal to the proton, in the nucleus
mcqs.why: The correct answer is no charge (0), a mass about equal to the proton, and it sits in the nucleus. Together the proton and neutron make up almost the whole mass of the atom. The electron's mass, by contrast, is very small.

mcqs.q: Almost the whole mass of the atom is concentrated in:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the nucleus, which is very small in size but heavy in mass because it contains the protons and neutrons. The electrons around it have very small mass. This concentration of mass in a tiny centre was a key conclusion of Rutherford's work.

mcqs.q: In a neutral atom, the numbers of protons and electrons are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is equal, so the positive and negative charges balance and the atom has no overall charge. The proton and electron also have charges equal in magnitude and opposite in sign. If the numbers were unequal, the atom would be charged.

mcqs.q: In the Geiger-Marsden experiment, alpha particles were fired at:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a gold foil. Most particles passed straight through, some were deflected and very few bounced back. From these observations Rutherford built his model of the atom.

mcqs.q: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. Rutherford concluded that:
options: Most of the atom is empty
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that most of the atom is empty, which is why most particles met nothing on their way through. Only the few that came near the small, heavy nucleus were deflected or bounced back. This emptiness is a central feature of Rutherford's model.

mcqs.q: According to Rutherford's model, the whole positive charge and mass of the atom are gathered in:
options: A small nucleus in the centre
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a small nucleus in the centre, with electrons revolving around it. The very few alpha particles that bounced back must have struck this tiny but heavy and positively charged centre. The rest of the atom is mostly empty space.

mcqs.q: In Rutherford's model, electrons:
options: Are at rest in the centre
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that electrons revolve around the nucleus. The nucleus holds the positive charge and almost all the mass in a very small volume. This picture replaced the idea of a solid, uniform atom.

mcqs.q: An element is identified by its number of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is protons: any element is identified by its number of protons, and if the protons change, the element itself changes. The neutron number can vary within the same element, giving isotopes. The proton number is therefore the identity of an element.
